speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unusual occasions demand that unusual actions be taken. I am sure the house will permit me on this unusual occasion, the celebration by one of our members of his fiftieth wedding anniversary, to mention this event. I am sure I speak on behalf of all hon. members in the house when I express to him, and through him to his wife, the warmest congratulations and felicitations, coupled with the hope for many more years of health and happiness.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. MEMBER FOR HURON ON FIFTIETH WEDDING ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister has said this is an unusual procedure to which we are resorting, but since we are the masters of our own rules in this house it ought to be possible for us to recognize a unique occasion. The Leader of the Opposition has suggested that since I come from the same section of the province of Ontario as does the hon. member whom we are recognizing at this moment I might, on behalf of the Leader of the Opposition and the members of this party, extend our very sincere congratulations to the hon. member and to his wife. We can only hope that when he celebrates his centenary, he will then be celebrating it under different political auspices.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. MEMBER FOR HURON ON FIFTIETH WEDDING ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:

This is a very important occasion, and it is a great pleasure for me to extend to him and to his wife our congratulations and best wishes on their fiftieth wedding anniversary, in the hope that they will have many more years of health and happiness together.

79951-0-331

This attitude is, of course, entirely consistent with the position which Canada has taken from the beginning of the preparation of the western position.
I think I may safely reveal that in the earliest stages of the negotiations we suggested that progress might be based upon comparison of the western and Soviet proposals with a view to finding common ground. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Justice based on a most interesting press dispatch by Mr. Harold Morrison of the Canadian Press, Washington, yesterday. I will just read the dispatch because it is most interesting to us, and then I can pose my question. It says:
New snags In Canada-United States negotiations have eliminated the possibility of beginning Columbia river power construction this year. United States authorities said they had planned to meet with their Canadian counterparts at Ottawa yesterday and today-
That would be Monday and Tuesday of this week, June 20 and 21.
-in what might have been the closing stage of a draft construction treaty, but the Americans were asked by the Canadians to postpone the talks until mid-July.
The said they could only speculate that the reason for the postponement was that the Canadian government could not iron out differences with the provincial government of British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the great importance of this issue and its interest, would the minister care to comment on this statement or has he any information he wishes to give to the house?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REPORTED POSTPONEMENT OF MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the fact that the hon. member gave me notice of his intention to ask this question. In reply I would like to point out that the information contained in the article is not completely accurate, and that the article itself indicates that it is based on speculation. I think the inaccuracies in it verify the fact that there is speculation here. The dates tentatively set for the meetings here in Ottawa were June 24 and 25, not Monday and Tuesday of this week.
In connection with this whole matter there are some problems, it is true, which are difficult of solution, as is natural in a project of this magnitude, and time and care are necessary to ensure that the best and most acceptable solution is found. In negotiations of this


kind, dates set for meetings must always, to some extent, be tentative, and no special significance should be read into the postponement of the next meeting which we now hope it will be possible to hold by or before the middle of July.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The meeting afforded a useful opportunity for us to discuss the problems occasioned by the introduction of jet aircraft into commercial service and the steps we are taking to alleviate the problem of noise.
The department is working in close cooperation with the air lines to solve this matter. There are no scheduled take-offs of civil jets between midnight and early morning, but due to flight delays of one sort or another there have been a number of delayed takeoffs during these hours in the course of the last few weeks. Discussions are being held with the air lines aimed at preventing this situation from continuing. A substantial number of other steps have been taken or are being discussed with the air lines as well, including noise suppressors on engines, the use of preferential runway take-off patterns to avoid built-up areas whenever weather conditions permit, and similar items.
Scientific tests have in fact indicated that the noise caused by a pure jet is in fact somewhat less than that caused by some of the current piston engine types, such as the Super Constellation, but the jet noise has a different frequency value and therefore comes as a new and troublesome sound to the listener who has not had a chance to become accustomed to it. I can assure the hon. member that every possible step is being taken to deal with this problem, and particular attention is

being given to means which will avoid jet take-off noise during the core of the night hours.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the committee is aware, the department's spending program for 1960-61 has been given very careful and extensive study by the standing committee on estimates. If hon. members will refer to the proceedings they will note that a total of 17 sessions were held from March 8 to May 12, involving more than 25 hours of deliberation. In addition to myself some 15 departmental officials were called as witnesses, including the two deputy ministers and the heads of many of our directorates and divisions. On the matter of emergency planning we were joined by my colleague the Minister of National Defence, the clerk of the privy council, and the director of the emergency measures organization.
In view of the comprehensive nature of the investigations and the fact that the minutes, which of course are available to the house, include my own lengthy opening statement as well as various working papers presented to the committee, I feel it unnecessary to make any general presentation regarding our estimates at this time. Instead, I should like to make a few comments on the very interesting and constructive report which emerged from the hearings and which has also been tabled in the house.
Before doing so, I want to take this opportunity to voice a word of thanks to all those who served on the committee and particularly to its chairman, the hon. member for Calgary South. Their helpfulness and co-operation were greatly appreciated. For myself, I consider that the discussions were extremely valuable to the department, and I can only hope that they were useful also to the committee. In any event, I believe the record shows that all the many pertinent questions put forward by the committee members did receive answers.

Supply-Health and Welfare program has any deterrent effect, the department will be pleased to review this subject with the provinces concerned. It is questionable, however, whether a comparative study of provincial programs with and without coinsurance charges would produce evidence to show that either admissions or the length of stay in hospital have been favourably affected by the use of such charges.
Regarding the committee's comments on staphylococcal infection in hospitals, I agree that any light which anyone can shed on this very difficult problem should be made available to hospitals at once. Here I might point out that in addition to investigations being carried out by a committee of the national research council, a great deal of work is being done in this field by the department particularly in our laboratory of hygiene and in our epidemiology and research and statistics divisions.
The report also mentioned questions relating to civil defence and the emergency measures organization. Most of the recommendations apply largely to matters outside my department's present responsibilities and have therefore been drawn to the attention of the authorities concerned. There are, however, certain aspects on which I might comment briefly.
For example, we are making every effort to accelerate the health side of the national survival program. An interdepartmental committee has been organized and has met for the purpose of co-ordinating the survival health responsibilities of the federal Departments of National Defence, Veterans Affairs and National Health and Welfare. The committee will continue this work and it is hoped that similar types of organizations will be formed at the provincial level.
As for stimulating provincial efforts in the field of emergency health services, several important steps have been taken in recent months. At the October, 1959 and April, 1960 meetings of the dominion council of health, the matter was discussed with provincial deputy ministers of health. A national conference on emergency health services has been held at which provincial representatives and delegates from national health organizations were briefed and the matter of establishing emergency health services across Canada was discussed. These various steps are being followed up by my department's emergency health services division, which is also carrying out its responsibility of assisting the provinces in developing their emergency health service assignments.
On the matter of uncontaminated food supplies, the special weapons section of our emergency health services division is collaborating

actively with the Department of Agriculture in developing means for protecting and decontaminating food supplies.
Active efforts are also being made to further the development of emergency welfare services. Here the main emphasis is on encouraging provincial and municipal governments to include such services within their regular departments of public welfare. In the case of five provinces this has already been achieved at the provincial level, and it is hoped that current discussions will have a similar result in the remaining provinces. I might add that my department's emergency welfare services division is collaborating in this work for which federal funds are available under the financial assistance program.
With regard to informational material, the department has produced over two million copies of an emergency welfare instructional pamphlet entitled "Your Emergency Pack". A further pamphlet, ''Welfare Tips for Survival", is now in production and is intended for people living in target as well as reception areas. Finally, nine exhibits have been developed with a view to giving emergency instructions to as many individuals as possible. These depict essential steps to be taken for survival.
In reply to the committee's reference to the department's general educational and informational material, I can only emphasize again, as I did during the proceedings, that this is a matter in which opinion reigns supreme. I would like to stress three points, however.
In the first place, our publications for the most part originate with requests from the provinces and are used to reinforce provincial educational programs. The views and demands of the provinces are, therefore, given considerable weight in our assessment as to the type and volume of material published. Second, on becoming minister I made a close personal survey of every piece of material which we put out. While I was not fully convinced of the usefulness of every single item, I did feel that the vast majority of the material was filling a very definite and legitimate need. Finally, the department has repeatedly discussed with the Queen's printer the question of charges for our publications. As a result we have gone a considerable distance in pricing certain items and in limiting the amount we distribute free to the provinces. The Queen's printer has been of the opinion that we have done about as much as we can in this direction.
But again I would stress that this whole area really boils down to a matter of opinion; and, as the house well knows, opinions differ widely on subjects of this kind. I would

not maintain for a moment that we are right in every instance, but I do think our over-all program is justified having in mind all the various circumstances which must be considered. I can assure hon. members that I will continue to keep a close watch on this important aspect of departmental operations.
I now come to the final area of the committee report which I believe merits comment at this stage. This is departmental efficiency evaluation. Here I was gratified to note that, in the words of the report, "the committee acknowledges that it was unable to establish any concrete evidence of a breakdown of operational efficiency". It went on to recommend, however, that the department request the organization and methods division of the civil service commission to undertake a somewhat more comprehensive study of the department's operations. While recognizing that we have already made considerable use of such surveys, it felt that more should be done in this regard pending the forthcoming general review of government efficiency announced not long ago by the Prime Minister.
I personally sympathize with this recommendation and would emphasize that the department has welcomed such studies as a means of obtaining an outside assessment of our operations. In my testimony before the committee I indicated that our policy of utilizing such analyses would be continued, and I now repeat this assurance to the committee. I believe quite definitely that such analyses could provide a very useful basis for any more general survey to be carried out with respect to government operations as a whole of which my department would be a part.
In its report the committee has expressed concern about a number of positions of similar classification in our establishment. It seems to me that this concern may arise from a misconception on the part of the committee, for which the department is no doubt responsible in that we failed to explain the situation adequately. I would like to clear up this matter with respect to the principal group mentioned, the 21 economists in our research and statistics division.
In years past it has been the policy of the civil service commission to use the general classification of "economist" for a variety of positions in this division rather than to create a number of special research categories. It should be emphasized, however, that this general classification merely provides an indication of the level of responsibility for salary purposes. It does not imply that all those classified in this way are assigned the same responsibilities. I realize now that in providing the committee with characteristic
Supply-Health and Welfare duties and responsibilities of economists used throughout the civil service we may have caused some confusion on this subject. But in point of fact the various professional positions within the research division represent an extremely wide range of responsibilities.
I should perhaps elaborate a bit on this matter. The research division services over 20 directorates and divisions in our health branch and four divisions in our welfare branch, as well as the offices of the two deputy ministers and the minister. Experience has shown that research personnel employed in a centralized unit of this kind can be used to carry out research projects for the various divisions of the department more economically than if they were placed in the divisions themselves. Staff time can be shifted more efficiently from one project to another to serve needs as they arise.
To my mind the research division has made a very considerable and comprehensive contribution to the department's operations. For example, a number of research officers have been employed in projects connected with the development of the hospital insurance program and in the continuing studies of hospital care involving expenditure analyses, cost estimates, assessment of hospital utilization and hospital services. In a program with so large a financial commitment these activities have been and will continue to be of the utmost importance to the provinces and to the dominion government.
As a part of technical assistance to the provinces, the research division has assisted in health surveys, and at the present time the director is acting as a consultant to the government of Manitoba in connection with its survey of hospital facilities and personnel. Two members of the staff are also acting as research assistants in the conduct of this study. This survey, which among other things relates to hospital bed shortages and to the need for chronic hospital accommodation, is the type of activity which the committee has endorsed in its recommendation relating to hospital construction.
I trust that these comments have helped to clarify this matter of economists in our research division. Since there has been confusion, however, I feel that the department should approach the civil service commission with a view to developing some more appropriate designation than "economist" for our health and welfare research officers. This we intend to do so that such misunderstanding may not arise in the future.
Mr. Chairman, I have now come to the end of the remarks I want to make at this time regarding the estimates committee report on our operations. Once again I want to

Supply-Health and Welfare thank the committee for its co-operation and for the various suggestions it has put forward.
I would like to thank the members of my staff for their loyal and dedicated attention to the department's business during the past year. I would also like to thank them for the assistance they so ably provided during the deliberations of the estimates committee. And, Mr. Chairman, may I conclude by thanking the committee for bearing with me during this rather lengthy presentation,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister need not apologize to the committee for the comprehensive character of the statement he has just made. He is the minister in charge of one of the important departments of government, a department that can satisfy as perhaps no other department in the government can one of the basic purposes for which government is established in a free society. So the minister may be assured that in so far as the Liberal opposition are concerned our well known dedication to health and welfare matters signals our approval of the time he has taken today in giving a review of the department which he administers.
I do not propose to follow the minister in detail along the particular lines he has chosen to pursue. When the individual items are presented there will be an opportunity for consideration of a number of matters which the hon. gentleman raised, and for comment thereon. I want simply to say that there were many things which I would have expected the minister to deal with in his opening statement. I should have expected him to say something about the criticisms which have been levelled against the administration, particularly in the field of social welfare, by the minister of welfare in the province of Ontario and his deputy minister. I should have expected the minister to make some comment on the position of the federal government concerning the question of medical care as particularly emphasized at the present time by the situation in the province of Saskatchewan. In that connection I should want to know whether the federal government proposes to give any financial assistance to the plan which the government of Saskatchewan has proposed. What is the view of the government of Canada generally with regard to this important step toward providing for the health of the people of Canada?
My views in this regard are well known. The views of my party were stated clearly at our last national convention, and they are in these terms:
We urge:
As a further step to implement health insurance provision against major medical, dental and surgical expenditures which combined with

hospital insurance would ensure that no Canadian would be financially crippled by illness.
It simply cannot be argued that no one in this country now can be denied the advantage of the best hospital and medical care on the mere ground of financial incapacity. We shall want to approach this problem, which I believe must inevitably now be faced, particularly in the light of the success which has attended the hospital insurance program in Canada, in a manner which takes into account our regional attitudes and needs and our financial capacity. The overriding consideration must be to provide our people with the most effective instrument against illness and ill health. To the extent that we measure up in that particular we shall give effect to the merits of our society as presently constituted.
The minister at the present time is without a deputy minister on the welfare side. Dr. Davidson, who has gone to another department, will no longer be available to the minister as his chief official in the matter of welfare policy and administration. I do want to say this now; that Canada owes to Dr. Davidson a debt which perhaps I am in a special way able to acknowledge and recognize. He was my deputy minister on the welfare side for 11 years, during which time Canada developed a social welfare and security system which I believe is comparable to that of any other country in the world. The contribution made to that development by Dr. Davidson is one which I am sure most Canadians will recognize, as indeed social workers throughout the world recognize, because of his outstanding talents and his devotion to the interests of responsible social welfare measures.
In this connection I should hope that the minister will see to it that the government does not delay in the appointment of a new deputy minister on the welfare side. That is, of course, a responsibility of the government, but I wish simply to say that the minister has within his department the talent necessary for the discharge of this important responsibility. I hope there will be no delay in the appointment of a deputy minister on the welfare side, because whatever may be the good intentions of the minister I am sure he will recognize that the appointment of a deputy minister will in itself be an indication of the government's concern with the problems of social welfare.
I am one of those who believe we have not reached the end of necessary social welfare programs which must progressively be devised in this country. I know it is said by many people, now that we are spending more on health and welfare than on any

other department, that the time has come when we should consider whether or not we have overreached ourselves. I recognize of course, that there are limits to what can be done, that there are financial limits. This does not mean that consideration cannot be given to future programs, or that we have not the duty to consider whether certain existing gaps may yet be dealt with. I believe that while there must be a balance between need and the capacity to meet that need, we as a parliament must recognize that we have by no means exhausted the things that have to be done.
I would remind the minister that when we assembled at our national Liberal convention in 1958, which elected our present leader, we not only dealt with the matter already mentioned, namely provision against medical, dental and surgical expenses, but we also urged that consideration be given to the extension of unemployment insurance in case of illness. There is now in my name on the order paper a resolution dealing with this matter, and I hope we shall have occasion to discuss that resolution.
In 1958 we also urged, and we still urge, the extension of pensions for disabled persons to include groups not now included in the disability program. We also urged the extension of old age assistance to unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age. We further proposed an improvement in the family allowance program with special reference to payment of the allowance with respect to children remaining students until they attained the age of 18 years. In addition, we proposed the introduction in new pension plans of provision for the early vesting of benefits, so that if an employee changes his employment he will reap the advantage of pension contributions previously made by himself and by his employer, so that in effect the pension would follow the man.
We also proposed that immediate consideration be given to a national contributory pension scheme co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement, an old age security pension beginning at age 65 to be based upon federal government contributions as well as on the contributions of employees, employers and self employed. That is an objective to which we must direct our attention. I mention it at this time because I believe we should not feel that all the problems of social need have been met simply because we have devised a social security program that is balanced and expanded. In this connection I would remind the minister that we have not heard from him in this chamber about the submissions made to the government by the Canadian welfare council in 1959 and in 1960.
Supply-Health and Welfare This voluntary organization of public-spirited citizens on two occasions in the past two years has met with the cabinet and pointed out the need that still exists in certain areas of social welfare, some of which I have mentioned.
They have proposed a number of specific improvements in the field of old age security and public assistance, blind and disabled persons allowances and unemployment insurance. They have also recommended the establishment of a royal commission on social security. I am not saying that I believe this is the best way to assess our existing program and determine what further modifications and advances should take place, but I am asking the minister to tell us what is the policy of the government with regard to the submissions made by the national welfare council. In spite of several questions that have been put earlier this session we have not yet been told by the government what is its view of the suggestions made by the national welfare council, nor have we had from the minister any satisfactory reply to the questions which were put to him and declared out of order the other day, when we were discussing certain modifications of the regulations having to do with residence under the Old Age Security Act.
I refer, of course, to the strong suggestion made by the Prime Minister in 1958 that Canada should embark upon a program similar to the old age survivors' scheme in the United States. I now wish to address myself to this problem. It will be recalled, if I may briefly retrace the situation in this regard, that in January of 1958 the Prime Minister announced that he had asked Professor Huson of the University of Western Ontario to make a study of the old age survivors' plan in the United States, a plan that provides for annuities or old age security on the basis of a fully integrated contributory system of old age security. The Prime Minister said that the study which he was then proposing would take not more than four months. At the end of that four months we were told without doubt, by process of implication, that the government proposed to embark upon a program based on such a study.
Of course the four months coincided with the termination of the election. The election took place, and we have not yet had any indication from the administration as to whether it proposes to bring forward a program that was so precious to the convictions and to the heart of the Prime Minister in January of 1958.
It will then be recalled that Professor Huson, on learning that he was to complete his report within four months, resigned saying he could not complete it in that allotted

Supply-Health and Welfare time. Whereupon Professor Clark of the University of British Columbia was designated for that purpose. We were not told that Professor Clark could not complete his report in a period of four months. However, when the election was over the government returned to serenity and we now know that instead of taking four months the report of Dr. Clark took well over a year. The report was finally tabled by the minister, notwithstanding the fact that we had some difficulty in getting him to table it once we had learned that the report had been prepared. It is a voluminous report and contains very valuable information, which I contend was always available to the minister and the government through the instrumentality of the officials in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
In any event, we have now had the report for over a year. The minister has had an opportunity of reading that report many times. Many hon. members, too, have had an opportunity of carefully considering its terms. We now ask the minister again what is to be the policy of the government with regard to this report on the program in the United States, a policy which the Prime Minister said would be forthcoming once the study, lasting four months, was made. He had said there could not be more than four months' study spent on this subject so that we could embark on this program. In the light of that background it is not improper or unfair to ask the minister, now that he has had a period of protracted study, what is the policy of the government. Is it going to embark on such a program?
I have before me in this regard the view of the minister of health in the government of Premier Leslie Frost. The province of Ontario has an interest in this matter, as has every province; because if we were to adopt the system in the United States that might conceivably affect the rate of contribution paid by the provinces to the existing universal scheme which we have now and which was established in 1951. I draw attention to what Mr. Cecile had to say in this regard. His view, as expressed on March 26, 1960 in an article in the Globe and Mail of that date, is the same view expressed by the Prime Minister in January of 1958. The article reads in part as follows:
The federal government yesterday was criticized in the legislature by health minister Cecile for failing to introduce a contributory insurance scheme similar to that in the United States.
The Globe and Mail of April 5, 1960 reported the statement made by Mr. James S. Band, deputy welfare minister of the province of Ontario. Mr. Band who comes from the city of Windsor is an old friend of mine

and of the hon. member for Essex West. The article reads in part as follows:
Mr. Band praised the old age, survivors and disability insurance program in the United States. He called it a well-rounded contributory plan that covers 93 per cent of the population.
He went on to call upon the federal government to do something about this program. What is the policy of the government? Is the government through the minister going to reply during the course of our discussion and say that the minister is continuing to study this matter? If he gives that reply- and that is the reply the minister gave us in the estimates committee and that he gave to me the other day in the house-then one can only conclude that when the minister says he is studying this matter he means that the government has no intention whatever of doing anything about this program. Or if that is an unfair interpretation we might conclude that if the government intends to do something, it proposes to do it at a moment it will regard as more advantageous in political terms.
I am the last person to criticize the government for having any such political motives in mind. I know the present Prime Minister would be the last person in the world to bring in legislation because of political considerations or because he hoped to gain some advantage in an election. As I say, I would not accuse the Prime Minister of that, but I have a grave suspicion that an exception to his political technique might arise this time and that he might be tempted in 1961 or 1962, or even in 1963, to use the possibilities of this program as a means of enticing an unwilling public to support him again for a second time.

If that is not the
situation, then the minister should tell us forthrightly now whether after his study of the Clark report he believes that the United States survivor program is one that is adaptable to our needs and to our purse. If he tells us that it is adaptable, then does he agree with the position we took at our convention in 1958 that such a scheme ought to be based on federal contributions as well as contributions of employees, employers and self employed? We are entitled to know where the government stands in this matter, and I hope that discussion of the minister's estimates will not conclude without his telling us, as I believe under our parliamentary system the government should, what the intentions of the government are. If the government feels that this scheme is not adaptable to our needs, let the minister say so. If he proposes to wait until an election, let

him frankly say so. That kind of frankness would raise the minister in the estimation of all his fellows in the house, and it would give us an opportunity of appraising the program itself.
The minister also spoke of civil defence matters. I propose to say little on that subject at this time but rather to wait until we reach the particular estimates. I would say now that while the minister continues to discharge his functions in a limited field we are convinced, with regard to certain outside operations of civil defence and particularly those having to do with the absence of any definite authority in the matter of emergency regulations and action, that the time has come when we should clearly know where the final authority resides in such a situation. Does it reside with the Prime Minister? Does it reside with the Minister of National Defence? Does it reside with the Minister of National Health and Welfare? Or is it clear that this point has not yet been decided?
If that is the situation it is, of course, a serious reflection on the administration of the government. I look forward to an opportunity on the estimates to discuss further other aspects of this program. I hope the minister will take advantage of these estimates to tell us frankly what the policy of the government is on a number of matters, particularly in the field of social welfare to which I have referred. I hope he will tell us what the government's position is with regard to medical care insurance. I hope he will tell us what the government's position is with regard to the United States old age survivor security system.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as recently as last week the Canadian people saw a very important step being taken on the road to proper health care in this country. If we cast our minds back to 1947 we can all remember that it was the same provincial government of Saskatchewan that brought into being the first hospital insurance plan in this country. That hospital insurance plan was fought very bitterly at that time. Any of us who were closely interested and who watched the struggle at that time can recognize the similarity in the viciousness of the fight against the medical insurance plan which the Saskatchewan government is going to bring in next year.
But we also recall that following that historic step in the field of health care, within three years the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia had both followed suit, and that after 10 years the federal government, through the process of an election and the acceleration of action because of a change of government, finally took the lead as far as
Supply-Health and Welfare the rest of the country was concerned, accepted its responsibility and took its part in the field of hospital insurance. We find that only three short years after the federal government accepted its proper responsibility six more of our provinces followed suit, and there are negotiations under way to provide hospital insurance for the Canadian people in the last province in the country that does not have such a plan.
Now we see a second step being taken by the prairie province of Saskatchewan. It seems very strange to me that one of the poorest provinces in Canada should be the one to take the lead in this field. Those of us who have followed the newspapers in the last couple of months realize the bitter fight they had on their hands. The program was fought most bitterly by the doctors' association in the province and, incidentally, the doctors overplayed their hand. They apparently hired advisers who did not advise too well, and as a result they made their position completely untenable from the point of view of any political party in that province accepting it.
Because of the stand they took they became more or less orphans in the field and in a way the fourth group opposed to the plans of the provincial government. The Liberals in the province did not say they were against the implementation of health insurance but rather said that they would hold a plebiscite.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They were against the government's plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They were against the government's plan. In listening to the hon. member for Essex East I was quite amused to hear him reminiscing about the stand taken by the Liberal party at their last national convention. I might remind him of the much more recent stand taken by the Liberal leader in the province of Saskatchewan, who expressed his opposition to the implementation of health insurance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Let us speak as members of the federal parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You are wise on that one, Paul.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am always wise.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The Conservatives in the province of Saskatchewan were not opposed to health insurance, but they thought the province might be better served by setting up a royal commission to investigate the matter. The Social Crediters were not opposed either, but they thought the public could be better served by having private insurance companies or private enterprise look after health needs.
5254	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Health and Welfare
I would say that the Canadian people are deeply indebted to the government of Saskatchewan for taking the lead in this matter, a lead that should have been taken by the federal government. I predict that in the period of the next few years, depending on how long it takes for the federal government to accept its responsibility, we will find, as in the case of hospital insurance, that health insurance, having taken firm root in the province of Saskatchewan, will spread across the country from coast to coast.
It is very unfortunate that the Canadian people are not always given a proper opportunity of studying both sides of the question of health insurance. I recall that one day earlier this session the matter of health insurance was debated in this house, and both sides of the question were very thoroughly covered by various people. Unfortunately at that time the Canadian public, as the result of some oversight or for some other reason, only received information on one side of the question through the medium of the newspapers. They received information concerning the fear expressed by certain hon. members that the implementation of health insurance would drive doctors out of the country and would increase medical costs beyond the ability of individuals to meet them. They received information concerning the fear that state medicine, as it was described, would inevitably lead to a situation where we would not have sufficient doctors to look after the Canadian people. In addition, it was stated that the standard of health care would deteriorate upon implementation of a health plan.
At that time, Mr. Chairman, I was rather surprised. Had the opinions expressed in opposition to this plan been those of laymen I could have understood very easily why the newspapers would not necessarily accept their views as against those of professional people in their own field. However, the views expressed in opposition were not those of laymen but opinions contained in the report of a commission set up for the very purpose of studying that problem. The findings of this commission were in complete opposition to the fears expressed in the house that day. Unfortunately it was only the fears which were conveyed to the Canadian public, and the report of the commission set up to investigate this subject was not carried in the newspapers.
Now, Mr. Chairman, health insurance is probably one of the most important of all the problems facing this country today in the social security field. We find that health insurance weaves in and out through the whole social security field and affects many other aspects of social security, as well as being

affected by the other aspects of social security. We find that over the last couple of decades a whole host of various forms of health insurance and hospital plans have grown up across the country, some through the trade union movement, some implemented by industry, some through nonprofit organizations and co-operatives, some by the doctors themselves and many more by private insurance companies. The greatest difficulty that we find with these plans is that usually they are too limited in scope, cover too few people or do not give adequate coverage or, because of duplication, the cost has been increased. We find that people are paying far too much for what they receive from this conglomeration of plans in operation across this country today.
Another very important reason for the unsatisfactory method we have at the present time for meeting our health needs results from the fact that the private insurance companies run these plans as a business, and as a business they must show a profit; that is only natural. If these plans are to be run as an efficient business they can only afford to insure healthy people in particular groups. The result is that the people who are in the greatest need of insurance are not insured, and the people who are insured have to pay too much for that insurance. I have always felt, Mr. Chairman, that there is something akin to ghoulishness in people or organizations making a profit out of the health needs of our citizens.
We have heard so much, Mr. Chairman, about how nice it would be to have a comprehensive health care program in this country, but where would we find the money to take care of the cost? I maintain that the costs would be no more than they are now. The only thing is that they would be honest costs. It seems to me that in this country we have a revulsion to facing up to a situation or a realization of what we are actually paying. I do not know whether it is because of the promotional devices to which we are subjected from the time we are old enough to listen to a radio or watch television, but we absolutely refuse to face up to facts. As long as we can keep the costs hidden, we think we are not paying them; we like to fool ourselves in that way.
I had an opportunity of reading an excellent article by Mr. Leonard S. Kosenfeld, M.D., associate executive director of the community health association, Detroit. He points out that in the period from 1940 to 1958 the amount of money paid through workmen's prepayment plans for health insurance in the United States increased from $100 million to $4.5 billion, and that industry's contribution had reached the point where it amounted to 14.7

per cent of the payroll or 32 cents per man hour worked. At the same time we find that only 27 per cent of the money paid for health care in the United States was covered by this insurance, $4.5 billion out of a total in 1957 of $15.1 billion. So you see, supposing complete coverage were given and supposing the cost were increased from the $4.5 billion which was paid in health insurance to the $15.1 billion, there would be no actual increase in cost. The only difference would be that the cost would be out in the open and people would recognize that cost for what it actually was.
I believe on a previous occasion in this house I pointed out-I think it bears repetition-a provision which we have in the Ontario hospital insurance with regard to what is termed temporary indigents, in other words people whose unemployment insurance benefits have run out and who have to fall back on the municipality for assistance. The municipality pays the premium for these people under the Ontario hospital insurance plan, and at the end of the year the municipality is reimbursed. However, the strange part of it is that the municipality is not reimbursed for the amount actually paid out but is reimbursed on a per capita basis. There may be two towns each with a population of 10,000, and one may have massive unemployment while the other may not. However, they both get the same rebate under the Ontario hospital plan, regardless of what they paid out. There are no strings attached to this rebate. The result is that the one municipality can pave the sidewalks and charge the amount to the hospital insurance plan. What kind of perspective can we get of the costs of health insurance when we have this sort of situation?
We also find in the remarks of Dr. Rosen-feld some further information concerning just how much coverage they really have at the present time in the United States. I might say that the coverage in the United States is much better than it is in Canada. I should like to read from his remarks. He said this:
The vast majority, covered by Blue Shield and commercial plans, are not eligible for general medical care in the office or in the home. This gap in coverage may deter the seeking of care early in illness, and reduces the availability of preventive services. Well baby care, medical inventories, medical advisory services and diagnostic services would, in general, not be covered by insurance. The fact that they can be covered has been amply demonstrated in those programs which provide such service.
The common practice among commercial plans and among many Blue Shield plans of paying the patient on an indemnity basis rather than paying the provider of service in full has led to serious inflation of medical care costs. This is largely due to the fact that there is no incentive for the physician not to charge the patient more than the amount provided for in the fee schedule. One
Supply-Health and Welfare measurable effect of this practice is the fact that between 1951 and 1956, costs of surgical care rose twice as much as the general cost of living. The result is a diminishing amount of service per dollar of expenditure. This is a source of concern to the community in general and to labour and industry in particular. It may have the effect of veto in the clinic of gains made at the bargaining table. Money expended for physicians' services is not available to meet other needs. Recent information indicates that about one half of the 15,000 union-management health and welfare plans in the United States are experiencing a deficit, largely as a result of rapidly rising medical care costs.
I quote that statement, Mr. Chairman, to point out in a small way the vastness of the scope of this field that I am discussing today. This is something that the federal government owe a duty to the Canadian people to grasp and to get their teeth into. They must remember that there are many interested parties and many interested groups in our country, many of whom have pioneered in the health insurance field and have brought it up to at least what we have today.
The medical profession and their legitimate interests must be well guarded and must be well thought out in any plan that we devise in this country for medical care. The hospitals must be taken into consideration. The insurance companies have filled the need in the past but, as I pointed out, I do not think they have a proper jurisdiction in the health field. If we are going to look at the over-all picture and take the proper government responsibility for looking after the interests of the Canadian people as a whole, I think the day must come when we have health insurance at cost in this country and not at cost plus a profit to some organization.
Non-profit prepayment agencies have pioneered this field, and I feel that use should be made of the vast amount of knowledge and experience they have gained through dedicated service by many people across this country. Industry has taken a lead in some respects, particularly the railway industry and the mining and timber industry. But again, as I pointed out previously, this action has not only tended to hide the proper costs involved in this field but unfortunately has also tended to build up across the country little pockets of vested interests which may in the long run hinder rather than help an over-all solution.
Organized labour have been among the first to become interested in this field. But again, as with industry, their responsibilities and their objectives have been too narrow and have been confined to too small groups. There has always been a tendency to look after their own membership and to say that they are the only ones for whom they are responsible. That is not good enough in this

Supply-Health and Welfare country. They may have two members living side by side, but there must be some responsibility to the neighbours living on each side of them.
Then there is a final group which is an interested party, namely the general public; and that is where the federal government responsibility comes in. Judging from past history in this country it seems that the role of the federal government has never been to take the lead in this field, in this war on sickness, but rather has been to fight a rearguard action against all the progressive elements in the country who have been trying to find some solution in order to meet this great need in our society.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at one o'clock for lunch I was criticizing the present government because similar to past ones we find that instead of taking the lead and showing some initiative in fighting the war on sickness and disease they seem to be dragging their feet down the road to health insurance and proper health care and we have to wring this out of them step by step, election by election.
I think it is time this government made some effort to put a stop to the sham and hypocrisy of the health costs we are now paying in this country. Here is what we are paying for at the present time; at least, these are some of the ways we are paying for health care. We are paying private doctors' and hospital bills. We are paying hospital insurance premiums. We are paying sales tax for health care. We are paying insurance plans and non-profit organization plans. We are paying municipal taxes for charity cases, provincial taxes and federal taxes. We are paying into crippled children's funds, retarded children's funds, cancer funds, mental care funds, polio funds, tuberculosis funds, multiple sclerosis funds, muscular dystrophy funds. We pay charity through our churches, through service clubs and individual charity. We have funds from industry, hospital funds and, last and far from least, doctors' charity through the doctors themselves. As the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, who himself is a doctor, mentioned this year in a similar debate, estimated, up to one third of doctors' bills are written off as charity to their patients.

I have listed this number and there may be more. Imagine what we could save in just administration costs alone by eliminating the duplication of services and administration costs which we have in this conglomeration of so-called health plans across the country. Probably the worst feature of all is that it is not doing the job. In spite of this multitude of various schemes and organizations we are still not doing the job.
I would like to know when this government is going to recognize that the nation's health is the nation's wealth. When are we going to make health care available to our people as a matter of right and not as a matter of charity? When are we going to start including the people who are completely left out now in spite of all this multitude of plans which we have? So far, unfortunately this Tory government seems no better than the Liberal government which it succeeded in accepting these responsibilities. I hope that before this debate is over the minister will give the committee some indication of just when this government is going to accept its responsibilities in this regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: By all means.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The hon. member has had a great deal to say about the health wonderland of tomorrow in Saskatchewan. I wonder if he realizes that there has been a tremendous flight of doctors and surgeons from Great Britain as a result of the introduction of a similar scheme there? We have hundreds and hundreds of them in Canada. They have gone to all parts of the world and-

speechtext: Order. The hon. member said he had a question. Would he ask it immediately.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my question is this. How does the hon. member relate this flight of doctors from this sort of scheme to the Saskatchewan future?

I would be only too delighted to answer that question. According to the Willink committee which was set up in Great Britain to look into this very matter, we find that contrary to this concept which has been built up across this country about this tremendous exodus of doctors from Britain there are less than 200 doctors a year leaving Britain out of 60,000, which amounts to something like .03 per cent. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few comments at this time on the estimates of the department. First of all I should like to commend the minister and his officials for the very good way in which they have operated their department and the way in which they presented their case to the estimates committee earlier this session. I have listened with interest to the speeches of both the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Timmins, and I will comment on them a little later.
Taking first the hospitalization scheme as it is now in effect in Canada, I believe that a good portion of the reason it has operated so effectively and well is the very adequate administration which the minister and his officials have given this scheme. I believe there are some wrinkles which still have to be ironed out; certainly in any scheme as large as this there are bound to be some. I believe that the hospitals at municipal and private level should have more say on the advisory committees. Certainly these are the people who are in a position to put forward solutions to the problem of overcrowding and to the difficulties regarding the provision of increased care for chronic and convalescent cases. They are the people who are going to supply outpatient and diagnostic services. In my opinion this is an area which the provinces should be encouraged to enter to a greater degree than they have done so far. Certainly I can see no reason why the province of Alberta cannot put outpatient and diagnostic care into its hospital scheme. This would relieve the acute shortage of beds which exists particularly in the larger urban centres.
There is another thing I should like to say with regard to the hospitalization scheme, and this has to do with deterrent charges, and with what the committee had to report concerning that subject. This is a particular problem in the western provinces, and when I use that phrase I include Alberta and British Columbia and, though to a lesser extent, Saskatchewan. Possibly the provincial government is not being penalized because of these charges, but certainly the people of the province involved are being penalized because they are not recovering their full share from the federal government with respect to hospitalization costs. I support the recommendation that a study should be made with respect to these charges, because such a study might give us a lead in deciding whether they serve any useful purpose.
Supply-Health and Welfare I also wish to comment on the Indian health services and the health services provided by the department for the native population as a whole. We in Alberta are pleased that the department has announced plans to go ahead with the construction of a new Charles Camsell hospital for the treatment of our native population in Alberta and as a centre for those requiring treatment in northern Canada. I have only one suggestion to make to the department in this regard, and I am sure they will take it into consideration. I refer to the fact that for a great many years Indians all over the country have been going to private doctors for care. Sometimes these accounts are submitted to the appropriate branch which deals with Indian health services for payment, but I believe the doctors are not too well taken care of.
We have heard a lot today with regard to health insurance. The hon. member for Essex East spent some time outlining what he would do, but I was a little disappointed that he did not supply any details concerning how he would bring the principles he mentioned into effect. That is, in essence, the problem. I do not believe anybody in Canada disagrees with the premise that all Canadians should have adequate medical care available to them. It is all a problem of how one is going to bring these ideas into practice.
I should like to put on record the principles that the profession to which I happen to belong has recently enunciated at its annual convention. I think these principles are reasonable, and I commend them to every hon. member of this committee for study. They read as follows:
That every resident of Canada is free to select his doctor and that each doctor is free to choose his patients.
That the competence and ability of any doctor is determined only by professional self-government.
That, within his competence, each physician has the privilege to treat his patients in and out of hospital.
That each individual physician is free to select the type and location of his practice.
That each patient has the right to have all information pertaining to his medical condition kept confidential except where the public interest is paramount.
That the duty of the physician to his individual patient takes precedence over his obligations to any medical services insurance programs.
That every resident of Canada, whether a recipient or provider of services, has the right of recourse to the courts in all disputes.
That medical services insurance programs do not in any way preclude the private practice of medicine.
That medical research, undergraduate and postgraduate teaching are not inhibited by any medical services insurance program.
That the administration and finances of medical services insurance programs are completely separate from other programs, and that any board, commission or agency set up to administer any medical services insurance program has fiscal authority and autonomy.

Supply-Health and Welfare
These are all worthy of note. The hon. member for Timmins had a great deal to say with regard to health insurance and I should like to point out to him that human dignity is the essence of humanity in my opinion and the more we lose our individuality the more we lose our status as individuals and as a nation. Socialists invariably fail to realize this and the harm it does, despite their sincere humanitarian interests.
A colleague of the hon. member for Timmins spent a good deal of time dealing with the health scheme in the United Kingdom.
I suggest we cannot compare medical practice in Great Britain with medical practice in Canada, because we are two entirely different kinds of country. In Britain one finds a very small area in which a dense population is situated, while here we have a very large country where the population is spread from coast to coast. Thus, in Canada we depend primarily for the adequacy and the high standard of care which our people receive upon the general practitioner, while in Great Britain they do not. This is an essential difference which makes proper comparison between Great Britain and this country impossible.
Nor can we correctly compare the medical costs which we have in Canada with those in the United States, as the hon. member for Timmins did by referring to a publication from Detroit. There can be no comparison of medical care costs between Canada and the United States because those in the United States are three to four times as high as the fees charged in Canada. I would point out that the medical profession has been among the leaders in supporting health insurance. These plans are all on a non-profit basis. As I say, the profession has been one of the leaders in experimenting with health insurance for Canadians.
Another point with which the hon. member dealt at length was an assertion that the federal government should take the lead in encouraging health insurance and such matters. I do not pretend to have a legal mind as great as that of the hon. member for Essex East but it was pounded into my head when I came here that constitutionally it is the provinces which have the prime responsibility for initiating action with regard to such matters as health insurance, and that it is only after they have come to a decision that the federal government can consider entering into collaboration with the provinces with regard to any such schemes.
The other important difference I should like to bring to the attention of the committee is the difference between the question of hospitalization, which is a service supplied by

an organization or institution, and that of medical care which is a very personal relationship between two people, the doctor and his patient. While you may be able to socialize hospitalization, provided you allow the hospital some local autonomy, when you delve into the very personal relationship between doctor and patient then I suggest that the idea of forcing it into one mold will not and cannot work if humanity is to progress.
One final word with regard to health insurance. We have seen the action of the profession in the recent election in Saskatchewan. I do not hold any cause for the way in which they conducted their part of the campaign. I believe it was wrong. I believe that doctors as individuals must take a greater part in the political life of their communities in all levels of government from the municipal to the federal and in this way contribute to the various political parties in Canada their views and those of their colleagues in the medical association. I do not believe that any organization including labour unions should have a party of their own and do as the profession did in Saskatchewan, that is, launch their own campaign.
I wish also to deal briefly with the question of drug prices, a subject which I know is of great interest to all hon. members and of particular interest to the hon. member for Skeena. I agree that this area needs investigation but we must look at the problem in a reasonable light so that patients receiving medicine will not be hurt. In other words, we must make sure that the Canadian pharmaceutical industry develops on a par with other countries, that our medical research program is not hampered and that there is no restriction in getting drugs to the patients who require them. Certainly there are areas in the developing of drugs and the availability of certain kinds of drugs which in my opinion require investigation. I would be very happy to support the idea of such an investigation as I am sure would every ethical pharmaceutical house in Canada.
With respect to the social welfare legislation, I listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member for Essex East had to say in this regard. I commend to the attention of the committee, the minister and the government the recommendation with regard to blind persons' allowances. It seems to me that the means test should be completely abolished in respect of this affliction. I have a particular interest in the question of disability pensions, having a number of patients who are now in receipt of this pension. I strongly recommend to the government that the income limitations placed on those in receipt of the disability pension should be at least doubled and this should be done as soon as possible.

I have encountered completely disabled people in wheel chairs who prior to the advent of the disabled persons' allowance got through by handicrafts or work of that nature. After the inauguration of the pension they continued working at their handicrafts or other work and immediately had their pension cut off by the provincial authorities. It seems to me this takes away the very meaning of the pension. These people benefit therapeutically from working in handicrafts or other work and enjoying the feeling that they are making a useful contribution to society. To rob them of this feeling has an adverse psychological effect.
With respect to disability legislation we have heard a great deal of discussion inside and outside this chamber with regard to the very strict nature of the definition of disability. I wish to draw to the attention of hon. members and particularly to the attention of the hon. member for Essex East a paragraph to be found at page 522 of the minutes of proceedings of the standing committee on estimates dated May 24, 1960 with respect to disabled persons' allowances:
It was drawn to the attention of the committee that certain provinces have introduced programs of their own which provide relief to disabled persons who are unable to qualify under existing federal regulations. Where an applicant is disabled and only employable at intervals, or incapable of working except under special circumstances, the provincial authorities grant relief through the Unemployment Assistance Act. Members of the committee were of the opinion that as the federal government pays substantial amounts to certain provinces through this act, a possible solution to the problem referred to above might be found if a similar action were taken in other areas of Canada.
I commend that to the attention of the hon. gentleman and suggest to him that it was the action of the present government in late 1957 when it removed the threshold provisions of the Unemployment Assistance Act that enabled those provinces to set up their own disability allowance based on employability rather than disability alone.
I think it is worth while reminding the committee of a statement to be found at page 116 of the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1958 relating to conditions under which unemployment assistance might be given:
The conditions under which assistance is granted, including the rate of assistance, are determined by the province or municipality.
Expenditures for both employable and unemployable persons may be included and the costs of maintaining individuals in homes for special care, such as nursing homes or homes for the aged, are sharable under the agreement.
I suggest that the hon. member for Essex East and all members of the Liberal party
Supply-Health and Welfare are a little late. This government did in 1957 what hon. gentlemen opposite were advocating in 1958.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The previous administration initiated the whole thing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
But it put a
threshhold on it so the provinces could not enjoy the benefits they would have liked to enjoy.
I agree with the hon. member on one point. When we look at social welfare legislation we should seriously examine a proposition which would provide survivor benefits for the elderly and disabled.
Returning to what is for me a vexing problem, that with regard to income limitations, the abolition of the means test at age 55 or 60 for aged persons in receipt of disability pensions should be considered. I highly recommend to the government that the income allowable with respect to recipients of old age assistance should be elevated a great deal. Invariably you run into situations in which you find elderly people prevented from getting out and enjoying exercise by taking a light job and doing the things they would like to do because of the strict interpretation that is given the means test and the rigid application of it.
I cannot speak for the rest of Canada but a serious situation exists in the province of Alberta. I have a great number of elderly patients who have given up doing anything. This is not good for them medically or otherwise. They are afraid that any income they earn in this manner will be deducted from their pension. I know elderly women who have ceased baby sitting because the welfare inspector was prepared to deduct the amount so earned from their pensions. I know elderly men who surrendered the jobs they had as janitors for Legion and other community halls and buildings in small towns in western Canada. They gave up the jobs because the small amount of money they earned was to be deducted from their pensions. Part of the reason for this, of course, is the way the regulations are interpreted by the provinces with regard to the amount of income that is calculated for the home they own and other capital assets.
It seems to me that we could do a great deal for our older people with respect to this very serious problem and it would not cost the government a great deal of money if we raised the allowable income under the Old Age Assistance Act and Disabled Persons Act and waived it altogether with respect to assistance to the blind. We could do something really worth while to encourage self-help which is the kind of thing I believe we need in this country. 1 know a great number of

Supply-Health and Welfare these elderly people, some even in their eighties, who would love to be able to do a little light work. They are physically and mentally able to do it but they do not, and I do not blame them, because they do not want to give up the security of their pension benefits.
Again, sir, I want to commend the minister and the department for having done a great deal for the health and welfare of the people of this country. The institution of the hospitalization scheme has certainly meant a great deal to the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and I should like to touch on one or two matters to which he made no reference. The first is the fluoridation of water. I know that last year I tried to get him to commit himself officially that he was in favour of the fluoridation of water and he said he was in favour of it in his own area, Stratford. But I think that if the Department of National Health and Welfare would go on record as being in favour of fluoridation it would help the cause of fluoridation a great deal in the province of Ontario and in Canada generally. In the Toronto Star of December 31 last there was an article to the effect that the federal government was giving new backing to the fluoridation of water as a safe and efficient means of drastically reducing tooth decay among Canadian children. Dr. H. K. Brown, dental consultant of the Department of National Health and Welfare, was the author of a report which said in part:
There is no doubt as to the efficacy of a mechanically fluoridated water supply containing one part per million in very markedly reducing the caries experienced in children born subsequent to fluoridation.
He went on to say that no ill effects had been observed by the medical and dental authorities in Brantford and Stratford where fluorine is present in or added to the water. Previous to that time there had been some investigation in three cities of about equal size, Brantford, Sarnia and Stratford. Stratford has natural fluorine in its water. I do not know how many parts there are per million. In Brantford one part of fluorine per million was added to the water while Sarnia gets its water from the great lakes and it has very little fluorine in it.
In Brantford and Stratford the results in children were about the same. From 1948 up to last year the number of children in Brantford and Stratford showing no decay or caries in the teeth had increased from 6 per cent to 44 per cent. In Sarnia the increase was from 6.6 per cent to 8.6 per cent. I think that definitely shows that fluorine has a very
[Mr. Homer (Jasper-Edson).I

marked effect in preventing caries in teeth. I might say that in my home town fluoridation of water was started in 1952 and since that time caries in teeth among children in the schools has gone down by 65 per cent.
