Yes. There is a consolidated school in my area and about half the children attending the school come from country districts where they drink well water with a natural fluorine content while the other half of the children come from the city where the water supply is from the great lakes. As I said before, the water from the great lakes contains very little fluorine. One would not need to be a dentist or doctor to be able to go into that school, look at the teeth of the children and know where they come from. I certainly think this is a very important matter because we know that caries of the teeth can lead to certain infections which have systemic effects. I know that an investigation is going on in Toronto as to the value of fluorine and I observe in today's paper that evidence is being heard in camera. I do not know why evidence should be heard in camera. However, that is a matter outside our jurisdiction.
But when so many associations have gone on record in favour of the fluoridation of water supplies I think the minister should state publicly that the Department of National Health and Welfare is in favour of the fluoridation of water. He may not think that this means anything. In the municipalities of Ontario people can apply to have a vote as to the fluoridation of water and in my town the anti-fiuoridationists did force a vote. They put up all kinds of signs outside the town to the effect that the water supply was contaminated, that it contained rat poison and was not fit to drink. This certainly hurt the tourist trade.
One reason advanced by these people was that the Department of National Health and Welfare at Ottawa had not said that fluoridation of water supplies was a good thing. I think the department should definitely take a stand one way or the other.
I was sorry that I was unable to attend the meetings of the committee on estimates, but I have read the reports of the committee. The minister referred today to some of the recommendations made by the committee and I was particularly interested in their recommendation with respect to hospitalization, particularly the overcrowding in our hospitals. I think the minister said that the department would not conduct a survey as was suggested. In my opinion a survey should be undertaken

because many municipalities and some provinces have no idea what may be needed in the future. I think some advice could be given by the department.
I believe a full investigation should also be made into the chronic bed situation and the provision of beds for convalescents. Most of these patients do not require the facilities of an active treatment hospital and in my view they can be better provided for in chronic bed hospitals or by the addition of wings to hospitals for this purpose or in convalescent centres. This can be done much more cheaply.
In recent years many insurance companies, and I think probably this applies as well to the regulations of the hospital commissions, stipulate that outpatients cannot get diagnostic procedures unless they are admitted to hospital. I feed that this helps to make the bed situation more acute. For instance, if a person needs a gastro-intestinal series he will need to be admitted to hospital in order to obtain these particular X-rays at no cost to himself. He will have to be in hospital from five to seven days. He could just as easily go to the hospital for radiology, have this diagnostic procedure and yet stay at home. I do not see why some movement has not been made by the health branch to take up this question with the different provincial commissions.
Reference has been made also to the fact that we should have more research in connection with mental health. I am in favour of more research here. I think much can be done. In St. Catharines, just to give an example, we have a number of beds available for those who are mentally ill. They are set up in connection with a mental health clinic, and people who are mentally ill are admitted to the hospital there. From observations I have made I can say that many of these people improve and are able to return to work who would otherwise stay outside the hospital until their condition deteriorated to the point where they would have to be committed to a mental institution. I believe that more work along these lines would cut down the number of patients in our mental institutions. These clinics are doing all sorts of work with shock treatments and with the newer drugs, and I believe that with proper direction many of these patients could be kept out of our mental hospitals. They could be taken into these other hospitals that are connected with our general hospitals, kept for a short time and after being discharged they could report to the outpatient clinics. A good many of these patients do well. I think a lot more work along that line should be done in other centres.
Supply-Health and Welfare
In addition to this I find that patients will readily go to a mental health clinic connected with a general hospital and occupy one of these beds for a short time, whereas they are very backward about going, or will refuse to go to a mental hospital unless they are committed. There is still a stigma connected with being committed to a mental hospital. I think a lot of work can be done for our mentally ill patients, particularly in the early stages.
There is one thing upon which I feel the minister should comment, and that is the content of strontium-90 in our food and milk supplies. I noticed an article in the Toronto Telegram of June 1, 1959 which said that the department was neither exercised nor panicked over the condition, which is probably right. I do not believe any of our scientists, and some of them admit it, know how much strontium-90 it takes to have a deleterious effect on our bodies, both genetically and directly in causing bone cancer and leukemia. I was glad to see the Canadian delegation proposing that we set up a committee of all nations to calculate the amount of strontium-90, resulting from fallout from atomic explosions, which enters our food supply. More work can probably be done along that line.
Since I am a doctor, and since the health insurance question has been very much to the fore in Saskatchewan, I think I should say something about it. I think I can best describe what I think about health insurance by quoting what I said when I first came to the house in January, 1951. It was my honour at that time to move the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I had this to say about health insurance as reported on page 10 of Hansard for January 31, 1951:
I am quite aware of the fact that most health measures come directly under provincial jurisdiction; but after practising medicine for over 30 years I realize that one of the main elements in connection with the insecurity of our people is the high cost of hospitalization and the expensive diagnostic, medical and surgical procedures so often necessary without warning. I have often seen life savings wiped out in a few weeks or months of unexpected sickness or accident. I cannot help but express the hope that we shall soon see the day when there will be available to all our people a contributory health plan to meet the cost of major sicknesses and accidents. We have many group plans that are fine so far as they go, but they are either not available or are not easily available to the large majority of our people.
I said that when I first came here in 1951. I can clearly understand the objections that the members of my own profession may raise in connection with this matter. I would be less than honest if I did not admit that I would prefer to practise medicine as it is
5262	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare now practised in Ontario. The doctors themselves naturally have a fear of the disturbance of the doctor-patient relationship. I must say from observations of the scheme in operation in Great Britain that I found this interference did occur. I hope the same thing will not happen in Saskatchewan.
Many doctors whom I observed in Great Britain had large panels of patients and they could not give them close attention, certainly not sufficiently close to make any proper diagnosis. The doctors' offices became largely clearing houses for sending patients to hospital. I saw that in two or three areas. Some doctors admitted to me that since they could not follow their patients to the hospital they did not keep up as well in the practice of medicine as they should. I could quite understand that. They were working hard and seeing too many patients. In the areas which I visited, there were too many patients and too few doctors. I hope nothing like that will happen.
There are more doctors now than there used to be.

I am referring to the time when I was over there, seven years ago. I know that there is a tendency to criticize the doctors, at least by the press and by others. What I say of myself certainly applies to a good many other doctors. I will say that during the depth of the depression and since then I have worked from 12 hours to 18 hours a day.
You still do in this House of Commons.

During that time fully
three quarters of my time was devoted to medical and surgical work for which I received and expected no remuneration. That was in the worst of the depression. It was difficult at times to get enough on which to live. I do not mind admitting that. The fees were not high back in the 1920's. The fee at that time for looking after a woman during pregnancy for nine months and attending her during delivery varied from $10 to $20, and it was mostly $20 when you got it. Of course, attending a delivery generally involved the loss of a night's sleep. I do not believe that over the years I have been overpaid, no matter what some people may say about doctors. During the depression there were times when upwards of 75 per cent of the people in some of the hospitals in Ontario did not pay their way. They were paid for by municipalities and the province. Certainly in those cases no medical man or surgeon sent them a bill. Many a surgeon spent many nights at the hospital-and I include myself-trying to figure out surgical problems in order to try


to go ahead with some surgical procedure. I do not think I am prejudiced, Mr. Chairman, when I say that there was not a time during the thirties and certainly during the early forties when the doctors did not discharge more than their full obligation to the people of this country. I will say this, however. If we had had hospital insurance at that time the doctors would have been a great deal better off but the country would not have been as well off. There were no doctors at that time who complained of that fact. I have stated my position in connection with this matter and the hon. member for Essex East has stated the position of our party. I should like to hear the minister state his position on this matter also.
That was a very courageous speech.

I have
listened with great interest to the contributions which have been made by the various speakers on these matters of health today, and I must say that I greatly appreciate the privilege of taking part in these discussions concerning the need for the appropriation of moneys for the purpose of improving the health of the people of our country.
May I say that it is my intention to speak about and to attempt to place special emphasis upon the need and the part that a physical fitness program encouraged from the federal level could play in working toward such a goal of improved health. I feel that there are practically unlimited possibilities in this field. I feel that I should at this time also acknowledge that it is generally recognized that the responsibility for this matter of physical fitness falls under the jurisdiction of the provincial authority, but I have long felt that more encouragement should be given from the federal level to encourage and assist the provincial governments, and in turn, the local municipal governments and the people themselves, in a program which would broaden and intensify their efforts in this regard.
At this time I wish to pay my tribute to the great contribution made by the medical profession in maintaining the health and thereby increasing the life expectancy of our people in these late years. I want to express my appreciation to the medical men for their latest effort to get our people to become more fitness minded. May I say also that I appreciated greatly the remarks of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson when he was commenting on the need for activity, particularly for older people. I have in my hand a clipping from the London Free Press of a few days ago which outlines a meeting

which was held in Banff, Alberta. I should like to read from this clipping which states in part as follows:
You will be healthier if you have some physical activity-no matter what your age ...
These were the findings of committees which reported Wednesday to the Canadian Medical Association's annual convention.
The committee on public health said that even though proof is lacking, "we are all agreed on the benefits to health for all ages which are derived from physical activity and participation in games."
That was the meeting of the Canadian Medical Association. I also have here another clipping to which I should like to refer. It is headed "Fitness Program for All: Children get Priority, House Told". This is in Toronto. The article reads in part as follows:
Health minister Dymond said yesterday the government's new physical fitness program will be slanted towards giving every child in Ontario a chance to develop mental and physical soundness, rather than place emphasis on the development of a small number of outstanding athletes.
In asking the legislature to approve departmental estimates of $92,195,000 for 1960-61, Dr. Dymond said this year's budget of $35,000 for physical fitness would go towards a small study committee to formulate a suitable program.
I have here another clipping which I took from an Ottawa paper a short time ago. It mentions a series of articles entitled "Keeping in Shape". The author of this series is Bonnie Prudden who is, I believe, an expert in advising women on keeping fit. I should just like to read one extract from this article. It states:
Keeping in Shape is dedicated to the proposition that no reader is too young, too old, too full of aches, too fat, too thin, too flabby, too lazy or too far gone to keep fit.
The feature is written by Bonnie Prudden, one of America's foremost champions of physical fitness. For years she has carried on a long crusade against limp muscles, drooping postures and joy-killing fatigue.	~
I also have here a copy of a resolution from the central fitness council of British Columbia. It is a long resolution and I am not going to take the time of the committee to read it all. However the meat of it is as follows:
It is requested that the federal government authorize action to recognize and support, in co-operation with the provinces, such a national fitness council, based upon the policy, administration and operational plan submitted with this proposal.
Mr. Chairman, I feel I can speak with some authority on this matter myself as on May 24 last I had participated in organized sports for a period of 40 years. It was exactly 40 years ago last May 24 when a ball team was organized in my part of the country to play other teams, and that was the start. The sports I have participated in include hockey, football, boxing, wrestling, baseball, a little softball, and in recent months the sport of curling and a bit of bowling. I know 79951-0-332
Supply-Health and Welfare there are many hon. members in this committee today who can vouch for the last two at least.
I have had some experience as an instructor in physical culture in my early days and I have often said since that time that what you eat, the way you think and what you do will determine what you will be. I am more convinced than ever of that as the years pass by.
I do not say this boastfully, but I offer this as proof of my statement. I have here a photograph of myself which was taken on December 22, 1924, at the time when I first started to be an instructor in physical culture. I have another photograph, a newspaper clipping, taken just shortly before I came here as a member, when I was acting as an instructor for the police departments in the city of Chatham and the town of Wallaceburg, instructing in physical culture, judo and wrestling. This photograph is taken some 30 odd years after the first one, and if I do say so myself, I had little difficulty in handling men who were 30 years younger and 60 pounds heavier than I. I say that as proof of the value of this work.
May I say that I have not had the opportunity to participate in these activities as regularly as I would like since coming here as a representative of the people of my area, but this experience here has given me an opportunity to make an accurate comparison of one's physical well-being when engaged in work such as this, compared to the kind of life to which I had been accustomed in days gone by. The opportunity to participate in organized sports at that time was of the kind which I found gave me considerable benefit, more than I get here. I have to make special effort to keep in condition as compared with those times when I was participating more freely in sports.
May I also say that I am one who possesses the firm conviction that there is great value in the kind of training-and I would lay special emphasis on the word training-that sports coaches and athletic trainers generally recognize as being essential to the development of physical and mental strength which is a part of the successful athlete. It develops self-reliance, self-confidence and self-control. It teaches one to think while on his feet under fire.
I am one of those who believe that health and strength is just as valuable and important to the average business man and other people as it is to the athlete, and that the same things which the athlete does in a somewhat modified form would also promote strength and health for the one who may not wish to participate in organized sports. The

Supply-Health and Welfare difference is that the sport often provides the stimulus and the incentive to the effort that is necessary to inspire individuals to do the things that are essential for their well-being which they would not do otherwise. To put it in a short sentence, one must work and earn and deserve his well-being.
There is another thought I should like to leave with the committee in connection with this matter, and it is that one can continue to participate safely and sanely in quite strenuous activities long after most people think it is safe for them to do so if they would continue to train their bodies for those activities. However, by the same token I would seriously stress the folly of attempting to participate in strenuous activities without training, particularly after an extended period of inactivity, no matter how expert a person may have been in his former years.
I should like also to draw your attention Mr. Chairman, to the part that physical activities play as a deterrent to crime. It is a recognized fact that there is not only a higher physical and mental standard among those who are sports minded, but generally the true sportsman will possess the higher ideal and more objective goal in life. This to my mind is a factor that is well worth considering, because when you stop to think of the many thousands of dollars that are spent on the administration of justice, the building and maintenance of prisons, and so on, it is not perhaps an exaggeration to say that if some of the cases of crime could have been prevented through the medium of wholesome physical activities the money required would be well spent.
I should like also to point out that the need for a physical fitness program on a national scale is becoming increasingly more important in this day and age when men are devising mechanical ways of doing the work which they did by hand in days gone by. As a result of the increasing nervous strain caused by the pace at which we are moving today I predict that there will be an ever increasing need in the years to come for something to take the place of the work that our bodies were intended by nature to perform.
As I have sat here in my seat my memory has taken me back many times to the time when that fine old gentleman-quite a number of hon. members here today will bear me out on this-the Reverend Dan Mclvor would march in here in what he would call his parliamentary stride and sit, I believe, in this self-same seat I occupy today. There was never an occasion that he would miss to rise in his seat and extol the virtues of physical fitness. He was a fine athlete, I understand, in

his youth, a good sportsman in later life and still young at heart when I knew him, when well on in his eighties in years. The last I heard of him he was still active in the ministry, which is further proof of the value of physical fitness in the building of good citizens, and I feel that his words and his works will live long after he has passed on.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a moment to point out the tremendous benefit that could come to the people of Canada from a dollar and cents standpoint if a concerted effort were made to sponsor a health program which would be dominion wide and in which physical fitness would play a prominent part. I feel this to be especially important at this time since the government has become responsible for the health insurance of the people. An ounce of prevention to my mind is worth any number of pounds of cure. I therefore suggest that the government give most serious consideration to the advisability of encouraging some such program. However, I feel that in fairness to the people and so as not to give them the impression that you can just pick this physical fitness condition off trees, the people should be told that they are entitled to that greatest of all assets, namely a high standard of physical fitness. However, to be fit will also require a bit of self-discipline, a measure of self-denial, a bit of the will to do and a bit of hard work. But for their efforts they will acquire a greater enjoyment of their work when they realize that work is a necessary part of their well-being.
It has been a great privilege to have been given the opportunity to take part in this discussion today and I trust I have contributed something which will be of benefit to the people of this country.

We in the C.C.F. believe that now is the auspicious time for Canada to move forward in the field of social welfare measures. There is a school of thought which believes that the welfare state has already gone too far and that the measures we have today are hurting initiative, but we in this group feel that these measures which we have today provide only a basic minimum of protection and are the foundation of a better life for the majority of Canadians.
Because there is widespread unemployment, because the government has balanced its budget on unemployment and a depressed economy, is no reason for the rest of us to acquiesce in the government's belief that it should mark time, forget about its election promises and do nothing of substantial importance in the welfare field. I think the people of Canada expected this government to go forward much more rapidly in this

regard than it has done. One of the pressing needs of our country today as we see it is for a vast increase in the pension benefits which accrue to Canadians upon retirement. We feel it is not nearly good enough to have a basic minimum pension given to everyone at the age of 70 of a mere $55 a month. Surely the minister would be the first to agree that anyone who is forced to live on an income of $55 without a supplementary income has not sufficient money to provide the very basic necessities of life, food, clothing and shelter, to say nothing of the costs of medical care should they arise. I think it is a disgrace to our country that thousands upon thousands of our elderly citizens are living in hovels, living in fire traps, and suffering malnutrition in this year 1960 because of an inadequate pension.
I had hoped that this government really meant business when it said it intended to embark on a greatly improved old age security system. As has been pointed out today by the hon. member for Essex East, the Prime Minister, when he was in the position of having only a minority in this house, seemed in great haste to do something for his fellow Canadians who were in receipt of old age pensions. At that time he was not only in great haste but he was convinced that Canada should benefit from the type of old age security they have in the United States which to a large degree is related to recent income and is not merely a minimum pension paid to everyone on reaching a certain age. After that appearance of haste we had a long delay in the final preparation of the Clark report. We are confronted with an even longer delay in the government's consideration of that report. The fact is that this government has a hard, calloused and inhuman attitude toward the people on old age pensions who have no other means of support, since the government has failed to take any steps to improve their position.
Before the election this government was very expansive in its protestations of generosity for the aged. The Prime Minister has indicated great sympathy for the people living on a minimum old age pension. Since then he has had the Clark report. The minister says it is being studied, but that means, to all of us who have had experience in this house, that the government is delaying, that it is procrastinating, that it is postponing the issue. The government is failing to do now that it is in office what the public expected it to do after they had given it this tremendous majority at the time of the last federal election.
We in this country need an old age security system which has embodied in it a type of pension system so that people neither feel
79951-0-332J
Supply-Health and Welfare bound nor tied because of potential pension benefits to a given industry, nor can they be cast aside and dismissed without benefit of pension when after many years of service a company finds their employment is no longer needed. It breaks one's heart to ride on the railways of this country at this time and to hear the sad tales of railroaders who are being unceremoniously dismissed without pension benefits after 25 or 30 or more years of service. These are people who have spent their whole lives working for the railroads of Canada, and they now find that in their declining years they are placed on the labour market without the benefit of an adequate pension program to which they can look forward within a few years. This is certainly one of the best examples of the need for an over-all security system in this country containing a portable pension plan which will provide for the best protection of Canadian citizens.
I think now is the time for action by this department in co-operation with other departments, and I refer particularly to the Department of Transport, to ensure that Canadians in our nation will not be placed on the labour market in their declining years without the benefit of a pension scheme to which they have contributed for 25 years or more.
During many years in this house I have taken an active interest in making suggestions for the increase and expansion of family allowances. Many Canadians raising families find it difficult to meet the expenses of a home and the family budget particularly during that period of earning power. Family allowances have been a great benefit to Canadian families. I think it was wrong under the former administration and it is just as wrong today for a government to allow an increase in the cost of living to whittle away and undermine the benefits of family allowances.
I feel there is a substantial argument in favour of increasing family allowances so as to restore the purchasing power of the family allowance cheque to the purchasing power it had at the time when family allowances first became effective in 1945. That would mean an increase of more than 50 per cent.
I believe, too, that the time has come when there should be an extension of the age for which a family allowance cheque can be received. I think the age should be extended particularly in view of the fact that many young people whose parents no longer receive the family allowance on their behalf remain in school. If family allowances were paid to the age of 18, or even better to the age of 21, while a child was still in school this

Supply-Health and Welfare wbuld be of great assistance in meeting the large costs of the education of a child at late high school age or of university age. I recommend this to the government as I did to the former government on other occasions as an expansion of our social security system which would be of great benefit to Canadians.
Much has already been said in this debate on the subject of a prepaid medical care program. I am pleased to come from the province of Saskatchewan that has shown great leadership in the field of health services in recent years. Saskatchewan and its people have the distinction of having formulated and implemented the first provincial hospitalization plan in Canada. Although it is some 13 years since the plan was first placed on the statute books of Saskatchewan some Canadians are still not covered by the hospital plan. Despite this fact there is now an assurance that this situation will soon be corrected.
The people of Saskatchewan gave the Saskatchewan government a mandate to implement a prepaid medical care program in that province. I express the hope that it will not be another 13 years until all Canadians in all provinces have the benefit of a prepaid medical care plan like that soon to he provided for the people of Saskatchewan.
The hon. member for Essex East referred to the Saskatchewan situation when he used the words, "with regard to this important step toward providing for the health of the people of Canada." This is an important step forward, a step being taken after a great deal of consideration, study and planning.
The reason we in the C.C.F. believe a .prepaid medical care program is necessary .for all Canada is that a substantial part of .the population is not covered by any plan .whatever and will have to bear the whole of their medical expenses in time of illness. About one third of the people of Saskatchewan are not covered by any plan whatever. There is another reason why we feel a program is necessary at this time. It is because of the increasing cost of medical services. With modern medical techniques being improved and introduced and with an increasing number of specialists' services being required, the cost of medical care mounts. This makes it difficult for Canadians to afford the kind of medical care they need.
There is a third reason why we feel now is the time for action in this field. That is the tendency on the part of many private plans to reduce the amount of coverage under the plan, or to increase the premiums, or both, and very often to exclude persons they feel are a high risk and therefore persons who are likely to be in need
IMr. Argue.]
of medical care. Private plans, good and valuable as they have been, have not provided the amount of prepaid medical care to which we think Canadians should be entitled.
The Saskatchewan program has been twisted and misrepresented in many ways. It has been called by our political opponents, state medicine, socialism, regimentation, dictatorship and other things. We feel the program has been and will be based on sound democratic principles. It will provide universal coverage. Everyone will be covered under the plan, not just those who can afford to pay the premiums under private plans, or those whose health record is such that they are accepted in private plans or those who happen to live in a certain geographic area or belong to an occupational group where they are covered.
The second principle of such a program is that there will be a small prepaid payment into such a plan. It is estimated it will cost approximately $35 to $40 for an adult couple with no cost for children. This would mean that in the province of Saskatchewan by an annual payment of some $70 or $75 a whole family would have their hospitalization and medical care covered. This would not be the total cost of the plan, of course, but it is believed that additional costs can be raised from general revenues within the province.
A third principle that has been enunciated is that the patient will have free choice of doctors. There will be no interference whatever in what is called normal doctor-patient relationship. The main principle of the plan will be that a doctor instead of sending his bill to the patient will send it to the central prepaid medical agency established by the government and from that agency will be issued to the doctor payment for the services rendered. A schedule of fees and costs will have to be worked out but I think there is every indication that doctors will fare very well financially under the proposed plan.
I am sorry to say that whenever the C.C.F. has proposed a prepaid medical care program each of the other political parties has opposed it. It was opposed and very bitterly opposed by the Liberal party. It was opposed by the Conservative party whose candidates said that if they were elected their government would establish a royal commission. In other words, they were going to duck the issue and shelve it as quickly as possible.
Nonsense.

The Social Credit party said that they would have nothing to do with it at all. They were completely opposed to any

universal plan which would cover everyone and all they would do would be to use public money to bolster private plans already in existence. Three political parties were opposed to a prepaid medical care program and the C.C.F. took on the field.
But these were not the only people who opposed a prepaid medical care program. They had the help of the Saskatchewan college of physicians and surgeons and they had the help of the Toronto Telegram. They also had the help of some people who found untold sums of money to use to publish scurrilous attacks on the government of that province and to issue a lot of nonsense and tommyrot to which the authors failed to attach their names.
They have become rather worn but I have in my hand what appear to be four pages taken from the Toronto Telegram of Saturday, April 23, 1960. These pages contain a number of articles by a man by the name of George Brimmell, Telegram staff reporter, about Saskatchewan's plans for a prepaid medical care program. I might say that this literature was issued freely and placed in the box of every boxholder in the province of Saskatchewan. There is no indication who published it or who authorized it to be mailed but it is indicated that the series is reprinted by permission of the publisher of the Toronto Telegram.
After the speeches yesterday I do not know whether this was a Tory medical axis in operation or a Liberal medical axis that had been arranged for the election or whether there was some insurance company money behind its distribution. But there are some interesting things said in these articles. One article is entitled, "Blood Boils Over Saskatchewan Medical Plan". Another is entitled, "Scalpels Out, Saskatchewan M.D.'s Fight Socialism". The scalpels were not out on this occasion for an appendix that needed removing but for the democratic franchise of the people of that province. On the next page there is an article headed, "Many Saskatchewan U.K. Doctors to Move if Douglas Wins".
I have been following the newspapers since the election and I have not heard of any doctors moving out of Saskatchewan. I do not know of any satchels being packed and doctors leaving. This afternoon the hon. member for Welland said that a number of doctors had left the United Kingdom. As has already been said in reply to him, this, of course, is correct.
I did not say that.

The good doctor tells me that he did not say it. My ears must have been
Supply-Health and Welfare fooling me. A number of United Kingdom doctors have left that country but there are more doctors in the United Kingdom today than there have ever been. I hope the day will never come in the United Kingdom, as in Canada, when doctors along with other citizens will not be free to remain in the country or to leave as they see fit.
In Saskatchewan we have the services of a very fine group of doctors who have come to Saskatchewan from the United Kingdom. If they left Great Britain to escape socialism and state medicine, it is a strange thing that many of them came to the Swift Current health region in Saskatchewan, the only area where there is a prepaid medical care plan, and that they have been practising under that plan. Their neighbours say that economically they have been doing very well and that they are exceedingly good doctors. In spite of this kind of scaremongering I am certain that the United Kingdom doctors now in Saskatchewan by and large will remain in our province, as I hope they do.
But this article goes on to say that if the United Kingdom doctors move from Saskatchewan "they will have to fill up the profession with the garbage of Europe". I think that is an uncalled for slur on doctors in Canada who have come from European medical schools which I feel in many in-" stances are among the best in the world. I notice that the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, who is a medical doctor, is nodding his head in the affirmative. In this modern day and age I do not think we need to attempt to divide the medical profession-
I agree with you.

-or any other profession or group on the basis of the country in which people happen to be born. There should be medical standards set, as I know there are, for all newcomers, and there should not be any slur cast on the basis of the part of the world from which these people happen to come. I think the medical profession themselves, and I still do not blame the majority of medical doctors in the province of Saskatchewan-
You killed that straw man.
What straw man?
The one you just built up.
The hon. member should know all about straw men. Apparently some of his people believed this fiction but I do not believe it.

Wheat straw.

Supply-Health and Welfare

I think wheat straw is a very good type of straw. A lot of things can be done with it that might compare favourably with some things I could say about the hon. member. In any case, I do not think it is necessary to attempt to divide the medical profession by this kind of slurring attack. I think the medical profession in the province of Saskatchewan has been badly led and badly misled by some of the people who have been giving them this kind of advice. Of course, they should know better than to go along with some of the propaganda that they issued. I have in my hand an advertisement in which a number of names of doctors are listed. It appeared in the Assiniboia Times of Wednesday, June 1, 1960, a weekly newspaper, but similar advertisements also appeared all over the province. The advertisement reads as follows:
In recent weeks, we have been increasingly disturbed by the numerous comments made by a number of politicians regarding a compulsory government controlled medical care plan.
The advertisement goes on to say:
We, the undersigned doctors, will continue to serve our patients to the best of our ability and will strive to give them the same high quality of medical care they have known in the past regardless of what may take place at government level. However, we will not participate in any compulsory government controlled medical care plan. We shall continue to conduct our practices on a private and personal basis.
This is another method of trying to influence the electorate. I do not believe this statement for a moment.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, are we discussing the Saskatchewan election or the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare?
I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the estimates.

I was endeavouring to point out how the prepaid medical care program had been misrepresented and attacked in Saskatchewan. Nevertheless, the people of that province showed themselves in favour of the plan.
Forty per cent.

That interjection is significant; it makes it clear that the people who voted C.C.F. were for the plan and those who voted for the other political parties were opposed to it. If you want to take the attitude that a political party has to have an over-all majority in order to implement its program, then democracy would come to a standstill in this country because very few governments ever obtain a clear majority from the electorate.
[Mr. Bigg.)

All Canada will watch this program with a great deal of interest. The C.C.F. in Saskatchewan is once again showing the way. But I plead with the Minister of National Health and Welfare to speed up the government's consideration of a prepaid medical care program. Let us hope the federal government will not take another 10 years to act on this type of program as the federal government took to implement a national hospitalization program. The people of Saskatchewan, because of the results of the recent election, will have the opportunity to enjoy the benefits of a prepaid medical care program.
I am asking this government to also show some leadership so that the Canadians in other provinces may have a chance to benefit from a prepaid medical care program. The federal government has a responsibility in this field, just as the federal government has accepted responsibility in the field of hospitalization. The Canadian government should come forward now with a federal prepaid medical care act by which the federal government would co-operate with any provincial government prepared to embark on such a prepaid medical care program.
He wants us to bail out the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan.

Nobody will need to bail out the C.C.F. This is a strange remark coming from the member of a party, the Conservative party, that failed to elect a single member in the recent election. It is not the C.C.F. that needs bailing out but the Tory party which has ceased to exist in Saskatchewan on a provincial basis since 1938.
Even with a prepaid medical care program we will not have a complete health program. The day must come, and it will come, when we have a dental program and a program which will take care of the costs of drugs. Only when we have a comprehensive national health insurance program which will include hospitalization, medical care, dental care and drugs will the people of Canada be able to enjoy a modern, scientific, health program to which every citizen has a right.

It is a pleasure to rise in my place today and find the chairman of the committee is a colleague of mine who represents a riding adjacent to mine. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speakers from both sides of the house who have spoken on the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I particularly enjoyed the remarks of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent who spoke about national health and fitness. I enjoyed also

listening to the hon. member for Jasper-Edson who spoke on these estimates, as did the hon. member for Assiniboia who just sat down.
Hon. members will recall that about a year ago I had the pleasure of placing on the order paper a resolution which read as follows:
That in the opinion of this house the government should give early consideration to the advisability of establishing a Canada sports council with the object of fostering and encouraging amateur sport in Canada, such council to have representatives from each of the provinces of Canada.
Hon. members will recall that on that occasion sincere and wholehearted support was given to the principle of the resolution. It was encouraging to me to find that the Leader of the Opposition and the representative of the C.C.F. group, the hon. member for Vancouver East, gave wholehearted support to that resolution. Again this year I placed the same resolution on the order paper, but for one reason and another I, along with other members, was not able to debate this resolution. Today, therefore, I want to speak for a few moments on that resolution as it pertains to the minister's estimates.
When I spoke last in the house on this resolution I referred to the fact that it was only a few years ago that the prime minister of the day rose in his place and gave, in a most refreshing manner, the reasons for the necessity of establishing the Canada Council in order to assist the arts, humanities and social sciences. The reasons advanced by the then prime minister for the establishment of the Canada Council could be applied equally to the case for the establishment of a sports council. If there was a need for the Canada Council, then I submit that there is an equally pressing need for the establishment of a Canada sports council because we are dealing with the health and fitness of the people of Canada.
We must remember that a nation's health is a nation's wealth. In glancing at the report of the Canada Council one would seem to find confirmation of the views and opinions of those who advocated the council. I noticed on reading page 20 of the report for 195758 that the council supported seven symphony orchestras and while the number of regular concerts given was the same as in the previous year, the number of performances for children and others was almost double, increasing from 93 to 175, while the total attendance increased from 320,000 to 477,000. I am sure that if hon. members were to give support to the establishment of a Canada sports council the first annual report of the proposed new organization would be equally glowing.
Supply-Health and Welfare
I suggested when I spoke before in the house on the subject that if a sports council were formed one paramount rule should be that the organization be as free from state control as it is prudent for any body to be that is entrusted with public funds. I would further suggest that the general rules which now apply to the Canada Council also apply to the proposed Canada sports council, with of course minor changes.
I also suggested, that a representative from each of the provinces of Canada be appointed so that the organization would be a truly representative one. The resolution speaks for itself in that regard. The persons chosen, as I mentioned before, should be familiar with the great problems now facing all athletic clubs and all athletic associations from one end of the country to the other. The persons chosen should be prepared, I submit, to devote much time to the youth of Canada who desire to play games in national and international competitions.
In my earlier address I referred to a few outstanding Canadians who would, I was sure, serve on this sports council and would give substantial leadership to the pressing and urgent problems facing amateur athletes in Canada today. If suitable persons are chosen, and if a reasonable fund is created, the indignities and embarrassments that have plagued our amateur athletes can be to a large extent eradicated.
In 1958 at the British empire games we gained one gold medal in rowing. In the final point standing we ranked fourth, well behind South Africa and a mere 100 points in front of Pakistan and the host country, Wales. At the last Olympic games held in Melbourne in 1956 Canada gained only 52 points to place 16th amongst 44 nations. What about the forthcoming games in Rome? We can only hope that at least once the Canadian flag will be atop the masthead in the Rome coliseum to warm the hearts of all Canadians attending. It would appear that there will be a large delegation from this country, and I only hope that we do well in Rome.
There are indications that we will not do so well. I feel that now is the time, before the results are posted, for some remedial action to be taken, so that at some future international show we can make a better showing. In 1958, in Davis cup tennis, Canadians played against a United States team that was virtually untested and the United States team made a clean sweep of the five game series. At the Pan-American games a year ago in Chicago Canada made a fair showing but in a limited field. May I say there was one significant thing about those

Supply-Health and Welfare games-I refer to the Pan-American games in Chicago-namely the fact that the Canadian Prime Minister was there in person. That was the first time to my knowledge that a prime minister had attended such an international event outside of Canada.
But not the first time a minister of the crown had done so.
I did not hear what was said by the hon. member for Essex East.
I said that was not the first time that a minister of the crown had done so.

The hon. member may be right but I think it was the first time a prime minister has attended an international event outside of Canada. It was heart warming, of course, to see him there. He certainly gave great encouragement and lifted the morale of the Canadian contestants. I am confident that under the inspiring leadership of the Prime Minister appropriate help will not be long withheld from our Canadian sports ambassadors.
At the 1956 winter Olympics in Cortina our Canadian hockey team was defeated by Russia. In 1960, as hon. members well know we had the opportunity of regaining the Olympic hockey award but we did not do so to the dismay, discouragement and annoyance of Canadians everywhere. It is for that reason that we should possibly plan now to make a better showing when we play again. That is possibly one of the reasons why I am urging the minister and the hon. members in the chamber today to do something about the situation. It is no sin to lose. I do not think that is what is bothering Canadians. What is bothering them is the fact that the nation does not go to sufficient trouble to assemble and train the best that we have.
We know what took place with respect to our Canadian hockey club. At Squaw Valley we placed eighth out of 16 countries. As a country which should normally excel in winter sports we placed behind such countries as Austria, Norway and Finland. We secured less than half the points of Sweden and Germany and we gained about one fifth the points obtained by Russia.
After almost all of the international events, certainly after the Olympic games of 1948, 1952 and 1956 and after the event at Squaw Valley, considerable publicity was given to Canada's inadequate showing. Generally speaking, there are many who say that we have been left wallowing in the wake of some of the more energetic countries which have become activated by the spirit of competition. I hope in the days to come we can


make a better showing. Certainly when you sit in these large stadia outside of Canada you would like to see our contestants do well and go to these international shows properly clothed and equipped.
In the last ten years many countries refusing the role of also-rans have introduced development programs. The idea is to encourage many to take part and from the many more super-stars as a natural by-product will be produced. These countries have also set up a centralized coaching system. Certainly a study could be made through the proposed sports council of Canada's athletic needs and problems. Canadians like any other group like something to cheer about. Certainly it does something for our morale both nationally and individually.
How proud we all were to be Canadians -and I can certainly speak for those of us in western Canada-that day in 1928 when the lean and hungry Percy Williams popped the eyeballs out of the athletic world at Amsterdam. He became a national hero, and in his home town of Vancouver, in particular, he provided the spark and incentive to hundreds of school children to take an interest in track and field. The result has been that Vancouver annually stages the largest track and field meet in Canada. That credit, as I have indicated, is due to one performer who did so well in an international competition.
How proud we were as a nation of Anne Heggtveit of Ottawa for her great triumph at Squaw Valley. The same statement applies to Bob Paul and Barbara Wagner who did such a fine job in skating competitions. They certainly inspired to greater feats the other athletes assembled and, let us say, the small fry on rinks and ponds everywhere.
Canadians at the winter Olympics were provided with an emotional thrill through the victories of the people whom I have just mentioned. Because of their victories and their examples will not hundreds and hundreds more take up skiing and figure skating? Does anyone feel that because of Barbara Ann Scott fewer Canadians became interested in ice skating? Is not the morale of Canadians higher and thus is not Canada a better place in which to live because of the great achievement of these fine amateur athletes? Take away national pride and what have you left?
What we legislators and the various government departments must realize is that our citizens are interested not only in these international sports but in sports in general. What we must also realize is the substantial potential ability of our amateur sport ambassadors in improving public relations around

the world. Surely Barbara Ann Scott, Anne Heggtveit and so many others have left a lasting impression upon the peoples of the world that Canada is a place of nice people and fine things. How else do you become acquainted with a country? If our few sports ambassadors have left a good impression upon the minds of the nations overseas, have they not made it just that much easier for our Department of External Affairs?
Mr. A. D. White, who I believe is not now a coach at the University of Toronto but who was a very popular and successful coach, delivered an address to the Couchiching conference and when referring to the Olympic games he said this:
It appears that in Canada there is little understanding of the professional calibre of this international sports show in which our athletes seem so poorly equipped to compete.
One interesting observation was this. Some observers have interpreted our results at the games as an indication that the Canadian population is below par physically. I do not go along with the general notion that we are well below par. However, I think there is a real problem to be met. If we are below par physically then something ought to be done about it at an early date. I am sure that all hon. members and for that matter all ministers are tired of the appeals being made to them for federal funds to assist travelling clubs. The creation of a Canada sports council would not satisfy all of them by any means but at least the athletic governing bodies would be able to police themselves better and the essential things could be taken care of. That is what the Canada Council has found to date. That council could not and cannot take care of all appeals but certainly some of the essential appeals are being taken care of.
During a relatively short period I have received as I imagine have all hon. members, letters from various athletic clubs throughout the country. There was an appeal made by the team that represented Canada in Moscow in November, 1958. There was the appeal of the basketball team that represented Canada in Chile. There was the request for funds by the Canadian grass hockey team that played in half a dozen countries in Europe in 1959. All hon. members will recall the general appeal of the rugby team which left from Vancouver and toured Japan and made so many friends there. It made an equal appeal for funds but unfortunately, like the others, received nothing.
We all know about the plight of the Belleville McFarlands and the appeal for funds for the Canadian Pan-American games committee and the Canadian winter Olympics committee. In almost all of these cases the 79951-0-333
Supply-Health and Welfare Canadian team was seen abroad either in stadia or on television by millions of persons. During the Squaw Valley games the Columbia broadcasting system estimated the total television coverage reached an audience of some 66 million people. The cost to the C.B.S. company was $2 million. This, I submit, is in the realm of big business.
The Minister of Transport when being interviewed over a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation program in Toronto mentioned that some Canadian athletes are better known outside Canada than most prominent politicians.
The Leader of the Opposition was denied a similar opportunity.

Yes, I recall that. I may say that I have long been a follower of the Leader of the Opposition, and perhaps on some of these sports programs I would find it a pleasure to hear about some of the events he participated in so many years ago. I am very pleased he took the time to support this resolution and I feel sure that he will continue to support it, at least I hope he will.
Mr. Chairman, if you agree with me that our amateurs now perform before millions of persons and have the fortunate ability of assisting us in so many ways, what, might I ask, do we as federal legislators do for them, and in turn for the younger sports minded people of the country? I am not criticizing in any way the present administration or even the previous administration, but from almost time immemorial the senior government of Canada has been obliged to reject about 99.9 per cent of all appeals for financial assistance save and except the appeals of the Canadian Olympic association, which makes an appeal every four years.
For the 1956 Olympic games this house provided $60,000. That was provided by the previous administration. When it came to 1960 the present administration provided the same amount of money. But I want to point out that the $60,000 in 1960 had to be spread over three major international events, the one at Squaw Valley, part went to the PanAmerican games in Chicago, and part to the large sports event which is coming up in Rome later this year. I wish to point out that we provide such seemingly small sums for these international events, whereas in the field of entertainment, for example the C.B.C., we provide some $79 million. We also provide upwards of $1 million to the national gallery and many millions to the national film board. I feel that some of these sports ambassadors are doing the same job
