Thank you, Mr. Chairman, it was a pleasure to speak on this subject again, and I hope the minister will do everything possible to assist.

While I was listening to the discussion a moment ago I thought there had been a cabinet shuffle and I was about to offer my congratulations to the new minister of national health and welfare. But I see now the hon. gentleman was only substituting while the real minister absented himself for a moment or two.
I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson and the hon. member for Welland, both of whom are practising medical men who have an intimate knowledge of the subject matter of this discussion. Many others of us can only attempt to understand in a vicarious way these questions affecting the health of the people of this nation. While, as I have indicated on other occasions, I believe that the health and physical welfare of our Canadian citizens is the most important national effort we have, and while the department, through its various branches deals extensively with the health and welfare of our people, I feel, especially in view of the fact that the hon. member for Timmins and the hon. member for Assiniboia have both dealt with the question of further promoting the health of our citizens, that I might, perhaps, leave further discussion of that subject at this stage and perhaps comment more extensively upon it when the individual items of the esitmates are before the committee.
I was interested in the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, especially his reference to the need for an investigation into drug prices. The

Supply-Health and Welfare hon. member also mentioned the methods of advertising used in the drug industry. He was referring, of course, to the ethical drug industry. I want to say that we support him wholeheartedly in this regard. It is to this end that I should like to direct some of my remarks at this time.
There has been a good deal of discussion in recent months instigated by the remarks of hon. members of this house, by the so-called Kefauver committee hearings in the United States and by the inquiry presently being conducted by the combines investigation branch of our Department of Justice. Out of all this there has been probably more public information given about this industry both by the pharmacists themselves and by the manufacturers than has been available for a long time with regard to what the industry is doing and what it plans to do.
One of the main reasons for what I consider to be the unnecessary high cost of drugs is that the ethical drug manufacturers-and I cannot understand how that word "ethical" got in there in relation to them, but it is there -are obliged to spend a considerable amount of money each year on research and in developing new drugs. The high prices therefore are said to be necessary in order that they may recoup the investment on research before the product is replaced by products of better quality, or of a different type or of greater effectiveness. Now the drug directorate of the department prepared a statement in March of this year for presentation to the estimates committee, and I should like to refer to part of that statement which appeared on page 2 of the report in so far as the question of research is concerned in relation to the drug manufacturing industry in Canada. Under the heading "Research and Investigation" the report deals with the administration and enforcement within the department itself. Then it says:
It should be noted that there is almost no investigation work on foods carried out by the industry or the universities in Canada and only a few drug manufacturers have research laboratories in this country.
Just the other day a booklet came to my attention entitled "Facts about Pharmaceutical Manufacturing" and no doubt it was sent to every hon. member of this house as well as to myself. It is published by the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers association, whose address is the King Edward-Sheraton hotel in Toronto. There are some passages in this booklet to which I should like to refer in relation to research in Canada. As to the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers association about which I shall have something to say later, I would simply point out that

it is not a Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturing association. They are not Canadian but claim they are and make some reference to it. On page 9 of the booklet it is stated:
As we have noted, it costs money to bring a new drug or compound into being. Penicillin and the Salk vaccine each cost $20 million before they were available to the medical profession in quantity.
The inference is quite clear, that the drug manufacturing industry spent $20 million on the development of each of the drugs, Salk vaccine and penicillin. That is not true.
The government of Canada spent a lot of the taxpayers money on the development of Salk vaccine.

The hon. member has stated the point I am making. The implication in the booklet is that this money was spent by the industry in the development of penicillin and Salk vaccine which is not in accordance with the facts. The discovery of penicillin had nothing to do with the drug industry in Canada or the United States. It was developed in the United States almost exclusively by the use of government funds. The same with Salk vaccine. The treasury of this nation put up the money to develop Salk vaccine.
In the United States it was developed out of the moneys collected by people through the march of dimes campaign.

I appreciate that the hon. member for Essex East has a thorough understanding of this subject and if he wants to enter the debate in a formal way when I have concluded the committee will benefit from his experience and he could comment without interruption. However, if he attempts to continue at this time his presentation will be interrupted by me because I have the floor.
I merely want to help, that is all.
The drug manufacturing industry in Canada did not spend one red cent on the development of Salk vaccine.
That is not completely correct.
I know the industry spent some money after it was developed. However, now the situation is worse. My hon. friend has left his seat and is half way out the door.
Now he is gone.

Yes, he has left. The booklet goes on to state:
It is estimated that in North America this year the pharmaceutical industry will spend approximately $200 million on research and development-

Reference is then made to the distribution of that amount of money. The sum of $200 million is a considerable sum to spend on research and development. I do not have access to the financial statements of the companies concerned but the following statement casts some doubt on the validity of the previous quotation. In the 1958 issue of Consumer Reports there appears a statement by Mr. Chet Shaw, director of the health news institute, who addressed the American drug manufacturers' convention in 1956. I appreciate that there is a difference of four or five years in the figures. With reference to the amount of money spent on research Mr. Shaw is reported to have said:
We've done a lot of talking about an estimated $100 million-
Spent on research. I continue:
-but we'd be hard put to document it. What if someone questioned it-someone whose voice we couldn't afford to ignore?
Most research work is done in the United States. Generally speaking the amount reported to have been spent on research is not very great compared with the portion of the sales dollar that is spent on advertising to sell the product. I have in my hand the United States federal trade commission's economic report on antibiotics manufacture dated June of 1958. It is their policy not to refer to specific companies by name because this would disclose information about the companies and they are simply enumerated as company No. 1, No. 2, No. 3, etc. The report reveals that in 1956 company No. 1 spent 8.1 of the sales dollar on research and 26.4 per cent on advertising and selling; company No. 2 spent 13.9 per cent of the sales dollar on research and 24 per cent on advertising and selling; company No. 3 spent 7.9 per cent of the sales dollar on research and 28.1 per cent on advertising and selling; and company No. 4 spent 3.5 per cent of the sales dollar on research and 30.7 per cent on advertising and selling. In other words an average of between 8 and 9 times what was spent on research was spent by these companies on advertising and selling. Therefore the reference to the amount spent on research has been over-stated to a large extent.
I return now to the booklet published by the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers association. They indicate that they are representative of 60 pharmaceutical manufacturing companies which are listed by name on page 20. By reference to Moody's directory and the industrial index I have discovered that only 3 of the 60 are Canadian. I find that 25 are subsidiaries wholly owned or controlled by United States pharmaceutical houses and others are subsidiaries of German,
22, I960	5275
Supply-Health and Welfare British, French or Swiss manufacturing concerns. When the booklet refers to money spent it is talking about money spent by the United States drug manufacturing industry, not the Canadian industry. The booklet also distorts the figures as I illustrated by referring to Salk vaccine and penicillin research.
In recent years there has been an intense and continuous search for a drug to retard the progress of cancerous growths and to cure this dread disease. I have examined university publications containing lists of gifts, bequests and grants and have here the one pertaining to the University of British Columbia. While it would appear that some contributions are received from certain drug manufacturing companies in Canada, in looking through reports of this type I have not been able to find one single instance where any drug manufacturing concern in Canada or the United States has contributed a cent toward cancer research in any of the universities of Canada. They may have done so but I cannot find that they have contributed a single cent to organizations such as the cancer research foundation.
I think it would be a tremendous asset to the health of our nation and in finding a drug or other method to curtail cancer if some of the money these companies say they are pouring into research could be directed toward finding some cure for cancer. It may well be that they spend funds along these lines within their own research establishments. I do not know about that and have not heard any reference to them doing so. However, a great deal of research work is done under sufferance through grants from government and individuals by the cancer research foundation and the universities, and I think the drug industry could provide some money for this work. They are not spending their money specifically on an attempt to make a major break through in the pharmaceutical field and do not have too good a record in this regard but are rather spending their money on developing additional uses for or refinements of drugs and pharmaceuticals that have already been developed to a great extent under public control.
I should like to deal with the question of quality control to some extent and refer to page 11 of this booklet issued by the Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers association. It will be recalled that its publication stems from the fight with regard to the purchase of brand name drugs or generically named drugs, the idea being that if you buy by the generic name you pay less than if you buy by the brand name, although that is not necessarily always the case. The association also says that generically named drugs

Supply-Health and Welfare are imported from other countries, notably Italy, where the manufacturers do not have the same standard of quality control as exists in the United States or Canada and therefore the drugs are of poor quality. On page 11 of the booklet I find the following:
The keynote of production and quality control is uniformity. The last batch of a pharmaceutical must be identical in every way with the first batch, even though years might separate them.
This leaves the impression that every time you buy a particular drug in a drugstore you are guaranteed that it is precisely the same in every way as when you bought the same drug four or five years ago or even longer. That is the impression they leave. They say that every batch meets certain standards over the years and that if I buy a certain pharmaceutical today there is a guarantee that in every way it is the same as when I bought it some time ago, even though I may not buy it in the same place. That is the impression that is being left and we know that is not so.
We know that variations are allowed by the food and drug directorate in their testing of drugs. We know that a drug may range from 90 per cent to 110 per cent or 115 per cent of the initial standard. There is a variation of 15 to 20 per cent from the norm set by the food and drug directorate. I am not trying to leave any false impression about the matter. I am merely trying to clear up what I think are incorrect impressions created by this booklet.
I know that some members of the committee are pharmacists and I am sure that the committee would be delighted as I would be if any of them would get up and give us their point of view because, so far as the drug question is concerned, I think they have been much maligned. It would be helpful if they would participate in the debate and explain their point of view as to this matter. As an aside, may I say that unfortunately for the pharmacist he is the person with whom the consumer deals. When a person is given a prescription he takes it to a pharmacist to have it filled and the pharmacist is the person to whom the customer pays $10, $15 or $20. Because the pharmacist is the one who deals with the patient, he is the one to whom the patient looks as being responsible for the high price of the drug. This is not so because the pharmacist is merely doing business. These are things that those members who are pharmacists could explain to us.
I should also like to deal with the question of advertising in the ethical drug industry. We know, of course, that the expression "ethical drug industry" means that they do not make drugs for sale directly to patients but for sale under prescription by a doctor

and through a pharmacist. Therefore they do not advertise in the normal sense of the word in that they are not trying to reach the consumer but rather the doctor, pharmacist or wholesaler, those people who are in between the consumer and the manufacturer. There is a difference in the advertising approach that is used.
While the advertising of proprietary medicines is, I understand, controlled pretty well and carefully checked by the food and drug directorate, advertising directed to doctors by the ethical drug industry is not controlled to that extent and there is no check as to the truth of the advertising. In this field perhaps I might call upon some comments by Professor Nickerson, professor of pharmacology and therapeutics at the University of Manitoba and Associate Professor Gemmell, associate professor of medicine at the University of Manitoba. These two gentlemen wrote an article which appeared in the Canadian medical association journal of April 1, 1959. It is entitled, "Doctors, Drugs and Drug Promotion". The article is five pages long and that is far too much for me to read.
However, I should like to make one or two references to the attitude and opinions of these two gentlemen, one a professor of pharmacology and the other an associate professor of medicine, with respect to what they think about the advertising approach of the drug manufacturing companies which, as I indicated earlier, spend from 25 per cent to 30 per cent of their sales dollar on advertising. Actually I have a reprint of the article here. I do not think I should ask the committee to listen to extensive reading but perhaps I might be permitted to make one or two references. I quote from the article:
A casual local survey during the past year revealed the following:
1.	A majority of physicians utilizing a "new" and effectively advertised analgesic did not know that it is simply the standard A.P.C. (acetylsalicylic acid, phenacetin and caffeine) plus a little barbiturate.
Apparently in the advertising this was represented to be a new and effective drug but was substantially the same as that which had been on the market for some time. Then the article says:
2.	Several physicians did not know the composition of the mixed electrolyte solutions they ordered by a simple number or letter designation. As a result, we have seen two recent patients with posttraumatic oliguria receiving potassium-containing solutions. Both died of potassium intoxication before renal function was re-established.
3.	A mixture of antimalarials and a steroid was administered for a dermatological condition without any appreciation of the amount of steroid in the mixture, and consequently without any

provision for gradual withdrawal to allow recovery of suppressed endogenenous pituitary-adrenal function.
Look out.
As long as I can wrap my tongue around them I will be all right.
You are doing as well as the minister.

I have been practising my reading. These are the results of the type of advertising in which the drug industry engages in trying to sell its products. It is something like an Alice in Wonderland approach; we will have the verdict first and the trial afterwards. As Professor Nickerson points out, it is the advertising department that will discover and establish the superiority of a particular product, not the drug manufacturing industry or the medical man himself. This is unfortunately the result of this intense concentration on the selling approach to advertising; the industry is trying to push particular products.
As I have said, I have only selected one or two excerpts from this particular article, and of course if we went into it in detail then the full article should be read, especially in view of the fact it is a scientific paper. Then my remarks could be related to the text of the article and a full appreciation gained of the points Professor Nickerson is making. I have quoted from the article because it refers time and time again to the advertising. At another point he says:
For example, the full significance of a recent promotional effort, which provided references to both efficacy and lack of toxicity, was not apparent until it was noted that the doses used in studies quoted to demonstrate the lack of toxicity were considerably lower than those used to substantiate efficacy.
References such as this are all through this particular article. I understand, Mr. Chairman, that I have perhaps run out of time. I had two or three other references I wanted to make on the question of advertising.
Oh, oh.

That is the democratic reaction of the Conservatives, as I have noticed them in many places. As soon as a member who does not belong to their party indicates that his time is up, they are quite pleased. In any event, perhaps they should show the same appreciation when the Minister of Finance is speaking. Perhaps I will have an opportunity later to make some other remarks on this important subject. Perhaps my remarks will promote the entry into the debate of other people who are interested in this particular field and perhaps as a result
Supply-Health and Welfare of our exchange of views and attitudes we might come up with a more successful approach to this drug question than has been the case in the past two years.

Mr. Chairman, I want to add my congratulations to those of other hon. members to the Minister of National Health and Welfare upon the splendid strides forward that have been made during the time he has had charge of this department. He has done such a good job that I hestitate to hold up the passage of these estimates. I hope he will excuse me for taking a few moments to speak on this subject because it is the only opportunity I have had during this session to make these remarks.
I am referring to the appeal for assistance for housing for elderly persons. I introduce this matter in the hope it will encourage the building of more accommodation for our elderly citizens by municipalities and service groups such as the Canadian Legion, Lions, Kiwanis and Rotary clubs. This is not to belittle in any way the progress that has been made since the limited dividend section of the National Housing Act was first introduced. In fact the success of these early developments has brought into being many such projects, sponsored by various agencies but all financed under the limited dividend section of the National Housing Act and administered by the sponsors. Since 1950 some 4,825 units have been approved and it is interesting to note that of this number 1,328 units were completed up to the end of 1956 and since that time, 3,497 units to the end of 1959; in addition to which there were 586 hostel beds provided in the province of Saskatchewan during the latter period.
The provinces in which they were approved are: New Brunswick, 16; Quebec, 993; Ontario, 1,837; Manitoba, 216; Saskatchewan, 860; Alberta, 124; British Columbia, 779. The amount of loans approved for these projects totalled $24,711,318, and the sponsors for the projects were as follows: city and municipality, 41; church or church groups, 7; private enterprises, 16; the Canadian Legion, 8; corps of commissionaires, 1; charitable organizations, 16; service clubs, 35. There are approximately 9,000 persons accommodated in these projects, including the hostel beds.
These figures indicate the growing interest in this problem by the people and the various governments. Indeed, the very acceptance by the public has only accentuated the need and desirability of this type of housing. What does this type of housing accomplish?
First, it provides housing for those who are in advanced years and still able to perform the necessary duties to maintain a home without supervision.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Second, it allows these senior citizens to have their own homes and live their own lives instead of living with sons or daughters who may be hard-pressed to provide a place for them or living in back rooms or attics.
Third, it provides accommodation at rents they can afford to pay, thus maintaining that feeling of independence which comes with the knowledge that they are paying their way.
Fourth, it gives them a feeling of security when they know they will not be asked to move at a landlord's whim.
Fifth, it gives them a feeling of content because of the design and comfort of the accommodation and the environment.
Sixth, it reduces the need for costly county homes for the aged.
Seventh, the first grants made are the only assistance needed with the exception of some aid in relation to taxes as the projects are self-sustaining.
Eighth, welfare costs in these projects are practically nil.
Ninth, it encourages the introduction of new sources of money into the housing field.
In this connection, I may say that the Canadian Legion branches in the Toronto area have been trying for some time to induce the trustees of the Ontario canteen fund to make grants for the purpose of erecting housing for elderly veterans or the widows of veterans. This fund still has some $470,000 which belongs to the veterans of world war I, and there is no better way in which to use these funds than to provide decent homes for them in their declining years. So far the appeals have not borne fruit but it is hoped that continued pressure by the veterans concerned will convince the board that the five cents required from them out of every dollar spent on such housing is the best investment that can be made.
I may also say that there are many trade unions that have many thousands of dollars in funds which could be spent for this purpose and not only provide housing for our elderly persons but also provide work for their members. I mention this to point out the type of funds that can be made available for this type of housing and encouragement should be given to the use of these funds for this purpose.
All of these points have been recognized by some provincial governments which made grants under the following legislation. In the province of British Columbia the act is cited as the elderly citizens' housing aid act and came into being on March 15, 1955. The main body of the act reads as follows:
Subject to an appropriation by the legislature for the purpose, and provided the plans have been


approved by the provincial secretary, the lieutenant governor in council may grant aid to a municipality or non-profit corporation incorporated for the purpose of providing homes for elderly citizens, to assist in the construction or reconstruction of low rental housing units for elderly citizens of low income who are unable to purchase adequate accommodation according to their needs.
The amount of such grant shall not in any case exceed one third of the total cost of construction or reconstruction: and no grant shall be made unless the municipality or non-profit corporation makes a cash grant towards the cost of construction or reconstruction equal to at least one tenth of the total cost of construction or reconstruction.
In the province of Manitoba the elderly persons housing act came into effect on March 15, 1956. The requirements under this act are somewhat more complicated but for the purpose of these remarks the following apply:
In the case of an elderly persons housing unit for two persons, 10 per centum of the capital cost of the construction thereof, but not exceeding $500.
In the case of an elderly persons housing unit for one person, 10 per centum of the capital cost of the construction thereof, but not exceeding $350.
In the province of Ontario an act to authorize provincial grants to assist in the erection of housing units for elderly persons came into effect on April 10, 1952.
The amount of any such grant shall be calculated at the rate of $500 for each dwelling unit or 50 per cent of the capital cost of the project to the municipality, whichever is the lesser.
The minister of public welfare may grant aid to any municipality to assist it in any project for the construction and equipment of low rental housing units for elderly persons.
This act was amended in 1952 as follows:
The minister of public welfare may grant aid to any limited dividend housing corporation that has been incorporated by or on behalf of a municipality or has been approved by a municipality and that has had a loan made to it under The National Housing Act, 1944 (Canada) to assist it in any project for the construction and equipment of low rental housing units for elderly persons.
The purpose of this amendment was to allow service clubs and other interested organizations to sponsor this type of housing and to assist in the obtaining of equipment such as stoves, refrigerators, Venetian blinds, et cetera, necessary for these developments.
I have been unable to find the legislation under which the province of Saskatchewan operates but from information gleaned from the report on social welfare and rehabilitation it would appear that this province has advanced up to 20 per cent of the total cost of housing projects for homes or lodges constructed by non-profit housing companies for the accommodation and care of aged, needy, infirm and blind persons.
I have mentioned these facts in order to point out that grants made for housing for elderly persons are made by the welfare

departments in various provinces. In addition to this assistance, most of the municipalities in which these projects are erected give substantial assistance either in the form of land grants or in a reduction of taxes. In metropolitan Toronto, for instance, the council makes grants to cover the cost of taxes over and above $25 per unit. These grants have been made and this assistance has been given all with the primary purpose of keeping the rents at a level the tenants can economically pay, and up until the last few years this assistance has been sufficient to achieve this purpose. Perhaps I should point out here that the rents on the earlier projects run from $18 a month up, depending on the percentage of grants made by the province. However, with the increased interest rates, cost of construction and cost of land, it is now impossible to develop these projects and rent them to people on old age pensions, war veterans allowances or low fixed incomes.
This brings me to the purpose of this appeal. In these days when it is so necessary to reduce the cost of government I believe that more attention should be given to increasing the value of the dollars paid out under social security measures. For instance, while it might be impractical at this time to increase old age pensions generally, grants to elderly persons housing would increase the value of the pensions of the tenants and assist the more needy section of our aged population. By doing the thing in this manner we would avoid what happened after the last increase was made in the old age pension when some landlords immediately increased their rents and so gobbled up the increase granted to these people.
The federal government has recognized the need for assistance to the provinces and municipalities by paying 50 per cent of old age security pensions, old age assistance, blind and disabled pensions; and it seems to me there could be no more worth-while assistance granted than that which would allow our senior citizens to obtain the type of housing I have been speaking about.
It is my firm belief that the costs of construction and financing of the more recent of these developments will eventually spell disaster for this plan which was designed to assist elderly persons with low incomes and which has worked so well and with such great benefit throughout the country, because when rents for this type of accommodation exceed $50 a month they are exceeding the amount which these people can afford to pay unless they have other income than the pension mentioned.
When I first spoke of this problem in this chamber it was my belief that perhaps a
Supply-Health and Welfare fixed rate of interest was the answer to the problem. This suggestion did not seem to be acceptable and so I am making the appeal to the same department that handles this type of assistance in the provinces, namely the Department of National Health and Welfare. This grant would be as in all cases, for the primary purpose of keeping the rents at an economic level and in no case to reduce the equity of the sponsors of such projects. Sufficient safeguards already exist to prevent the abuse of this type of assistance.
We cannot praise too highly the work being done by members of the limited dividend companies who sponsor and administer these projects, all of whom serve in an honourary capacity and who must be really dedicated to the work to which they are committed. The best way for this government and this committee to acknowledge the splendid work being done by these citizens, and to encourage others to do likewise, is to give them a tangible expression of our appreciation by making grants in the form I have mentioned. To this end I earnestly solicit the government's favourable consideration of this appeal.

I have always been interested in health and welfare, and the older I grow the more my interest intensifies. First of all, before going on with the few remarks I wish to make, I must express my appreciation for the courtesy that has been extended to me by the minister when I have taken any matter up with him or have raised any question in the house. I must also express the appreciation of this group for the excellent work being done by his two deputies and his competent staff. The minister's staff in Ottawa and throughout Canada carries on quietly this excellent work, with all its ramifications and many divisions, and does so without glamour. I do not want to be misunderstood, Mr. Chairman. I am not suggesting that the department has not within it individuals with glamour. What I am suggesting is that its work is carried on officially without glamour. I have heard it whispered that there are members of the staff of the minister's department whose glamour is in such evidence that they have actually influenced the attitude of committees of the House of Commons. I therefore do not want to be misunderstood. When I say "without glamour", I mean as far as the scientific, administrative and technical work of the department is concerned.
By the way, in looking around, I am somewhat inspired and flattered by having a lady in front of me, one to the right of me and one to the left of me, all listening raptly while I volley and thunder. So I have a good start now.

Supply-Health and Welfare
The first movements in the direction of the modern state health, health insurance and other welfare plans and ramifications appeared toward the middle and latter part of the Victorian period in western Europe, and had their beginnings in Great Britain prior to 1900. Why? Because there were many new problems created in the development of industrial society and the increasing densities of population which were not so apparent previously. New conditions of poverty were created as the result of the development of industrial society which did not exist even under feudalism, where, with the exception in the case of crop failures, the people had a roof over their heads and good and sufficient plain food to eat.
It came to fruition with increasing rapidity after the turn of the century. While I appreciate that we must give credit to those persons in Great Britain w-ho had some influence in other countries of the British commonwealth, such as Kier Hardie-
And Cadbury.

Yes, Cadbury and Lloyd George. They were a small and devoted group of Labour and Liberal members of parliament to whom the British people owe a great deal in the development of their social security system.
The first legislation in Great Britain was in 1911 when there was passed the national insurance act. I read about that with interest at the time and I read some of the debates. That act was inspired by the activities of this small group led by the Right Hon. Lloyd George, assisted by people like George Bernard Shaw, the Cadburys, the Rowntrees, the Fry's and all the Quaker families who took some interest in social welfare in Great Britain at that time.
However, as far as Canada is concerned there has been a somewhat slower development, and understandably so. First of all, we have a more difficult problem in a country like Canada than in a unitary state like Great Britain to establish an over-all security scheme on a national basis. Our industrial development was later. We had a pioneer society much later than in Great Britain; in fact it has not entirely gone today, although I must say the spirit has gone in some quarters.
Anyway, the first official recognition by a political party of this question was at the famous Liberal convention of 1919. I do not think the hon. member for Essex East was in attendance. Possibly there might have been a little better result if he had been in attendance. But that was the first official recognition of the problem in Canada, and

we all know about the famous resolution which was passed at that convention.
However, very little was done, except in very limited national, provincial and municipal spheres, to look after the poverty stricken and those people next door who were going to the Salvation Army or rescue organizations, and things of that kind.
Then we had the Rowell-Sirois report of 1940. War brought about an interest in this subject. Then we had the Marsh report of 1943 and the House of Commons special committee on social security in 1944. I am sure the hon. member for Essex East was a member of that committee and took a very active part in it. Then the latest was the Clark report, which was tabled in the house on May 5, 1959, and according to the Prime Minister is still under study.
I had the report sent to my office, like other hon. members, but I simply did not have the time to wade through all that material so I took advantage of the opportunity to purchase a condensed copy of the report issued by the Canadian welfare council. I should like to congratulate them upon providing that condensed report because it is an excellent piece of work and contains the essential features of the other rather massive report. One can digest the facts contained in the condensed version very easily.
There was a great fanfare when the person was appointed who was going to make the investigation. He was told to do it as quickly as possible, but it took longer than expected. There is no doubt that a great deal of information is contained in the report which could have been obtained from the department. I am sure the former minister of national health and welfare will agree with me on that. Other information was gathered together, and I do not want to belittle anyone's efforts in this respect, but after all this fanfare we got a massive report without any recommendations contained in it. There were a few evaluations and hints and timid suggestions in various paragraphs but no definite recommendations, and we are still awaiting the decision of the minister and the government who are studying this report.
In addition to that I am safe in saying that studies of the reports have been conducted over quite a period of years by other professional and public bodies interested in helping Canada. I would also give credit to the work which has been done by prior governments. But it has all been done on a piecemeal basis, and possibly no one is to blame for that in view of the fact that these things have to be sold. They have to obtain common acceptance. Provinces have to be

dealt with and, as I said before, it is not quite as simple as dealing with this matter in a unitary state such as Great Britain or some of the other states in western Europe.
Then we have old age pensions, and hon. members will remember that the late J. S. Woodsworth was a very prominent figure in this sphere. We have had family allowances, unemployment insurance and health grants given us by the former Liberal government; and I have no hesitation in saying that I am quite confident that when the former minister of national health and welfare arrived here as one of the more radical members of the Liberal party, I think in 1935, he was one of the more aggressive members of that party at that time who did everything he could to urge the government in power to take action along the lines which was later taken with respect to family allowance, unemployment insurance, health grants and so on.
That was a step forward and this legislation has been of great benefit to many people. But the big weakness today is that this has all been done on a piecemeal basis and we in the C.C.F. group say that what we want is an over-all social security system in Canada.
This action which was taken by the former government was spurred on by representations from farmers organizations, labour organizations, women's organizations, various groups from universities and various other devoted groups throughout Canada as well as devoted individuals who all took an interest in this problem throughout the years. Today we have on the statute books the legislation which' was passed by this parliament, largely under the auspices of the former Liberal government. In that respect at least they were following up the traditions of the Right Hon. Lloyd George.
However, we say that more should be done and that more should have been done prior to this. Up to a few years ago people were opposed to over-all security and national health insurance on financial grounds. They said it was impracticable, impossible. That phase has passed entirely as the result of the experience in Great Britain. We all recognize the accomplishments of the British health service and legislation providing over-all security. No aspect of the peaceful revolution brought about by the British Labour government is more dramatic than their health services legislation and their social security legislation, and X must say that is to the everlasting credit of the pioneers I mentioned previously.
The Labour government which was elected after 1945 gave, I think, the lead to the British commonwealth of nations with respect to national health insurance and social security. In a matter of a few years the old style
Supply-Health and Welfare fee for sickness system has been converted into a new style socialist free health service.
Whether hon. members like it or not, a free health service available to everyone in Britain, including visitors, is accepted beyond doubt and there is no need to search for socialist opinion in support of this view. I want to quote two authorities to indicate how solidly this idea is based in Britain and in the west European countries and how great is the need for action on the part of the present government. I have read some of Sir Winston Churchill's speeches when he was a member of the Tory party early in the century, and the Tory party took a very strong stand against suggestions by various Labour and Liberal members such as I have mentioned. But I want to read a quotation from the converted Right Hon. Winston Churchill. He said in the United Kingdom House of Commons in March of 1943-and the war had a definite impact on the thinking of even Conservatives in Britain and most countries with respect to this question:
Anyone can see what large savings there will be in administration once the whole process of insurance has become unified, compulsory and national.
Here is a real opportunity for what I once called "bringing the magic of averages to the rescue of millions." Therefore you must rank me and my colleagues as strong partisans of national compulsory insurance for all classes, for all purposes, from the cradle to the grave.
I quote that statement with some relish because you still get a remnant of Victorian sentiment criticizing people who suggest that when we aim to produce security from the cradle to the grave we are going to make a soft, coddled nation. Here is one of the most distinguished figures in our history, and one who cannot be accused of coddling anyone, recognising that in an industrial society this type of overall security is imperative and necessary.
I also want to quote from the London correspondent of the Wall Street Journal of November 27, 1951 just after the Labour government had been elected in Great Britain. This is what I read:
-one pillar of socialism-'socialized medicine'- is certain to remain intact. .. The "free" health service set up by the late Labour government is so popular that it can no longer be made a political issue here.
Now I want to tell the committee of an interesting conversation I had with Mr. Rab Butler, who was, I think, at that time chancellor of the exchequer. Mr. Butler, in addition to being a very charming individual, is a very progressive type of Conservative which is more than I can say for some members of the Conservative party we see on the opposite side of the house. British Conservatives are really progressive both in national and international affairs and I am sorry I

Supply-Health and Welfare cannot say the same of all the Progressive Conservative party members who sit in this chamber. I was chaffing him about the attitude of the Tory party when I was a boy, a long time ago, about its antagonism to over-all social security and national health insurance. I said: Mr. Butler what is the attitude of the Conservative party now? This was shortly after the election in 1950 or 1951; I am not sure of the date. I asked him what the attitude of the party was then in view of its record with regard to the national health insurance and over-all security legislation which the Labour government had built up. He said: Mr. Herridge, the national health insurance plan and social security in Great Britain meets a need in a modern industrial society. It has served a great purpose and it is performing a great function in the nation. Its retention is demanded by the great majority of the British people. When you ask me to tell you what is the policy of the Conservative party with respect to national health insurance and social security, I simply put it in these words: It is the aim of the Conservative party in Great Britain to continue to improve it.
I offer that suggestion to the minister and his colleagues when they come to deal with legislation concerning old age pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances and other pension legislation which is sought and which is considered desirable for the welfare of Canadians.
Having said that, I want to go off on a somewhat different tack from the one which is usually expected of an hon. member speaking on these estimates. I do it because of my work with a certain organization which has not received sufficient recognition from this chamber or from Canada generally. I refer to the Canadian welfare council of which I have been a member for some years. As a matter of fact, I have taken a good deal of interest in health insurance and welfare services for many years. I was a director of a hospital for 18 years and I have been on relief committees during the depression. In addition I have operated a sort of one-man welfare service on occasions.
On one occasion, in order that hon. members may be able to see the type of assistance which I was able to provide, may I say a young lady wrote to me asking for assistance in deciding which of two young men she should marry. It appears she was in love with both. I wrote to her saying that I did not wish to risk either her future or my own by advising her definitely in favour of one or the other of the candidates for her affection. But I did eventually advise her to observe a cooling off period of six months, at the end of which time I felt confident she would be in a better position to make up

her own mind. As a matter of fact this was exactly what she did. I forgot all about this incident until I was on a visit to a town in my constituency, and as I was coming out of one of the public buildings a young lady rushed up to me and said: You are Mr. Herridge aren't you? I said I was, and she said to me: I want to thank you for the wonderful advice you gave me. Then she took me over to her car which was nearby and there in the back were four children.
That is just by way of example of the manner in which I sometimes function as an unofficial welfare officer. Perhaps I might tell the committee of another occasion on which I was able to be of assistance to people in difficulty with the welfare authorities. I can recall an occasion when a small farmer was being questioned by a relief officer. The man was in possession of a few cows-four or five cows, I believe-and a small quantity of hay. The relief officer was pressing the owner of the cows to explain why he did not sell the hay. I said: He uses the hay to feed the cows, and the officer said: Oh, I did not think of that.
But I see my time is slipping away, and I want to put on record the basic principles of the welfare council which I think are worth putting on the record:
The responsibility of government to provide financial assistance to those lacking the basic necessities of life should be stated in legislation. Such legislation should, among other things, define eligibility for assistance and provide for the establishment of eligibility tests. This would aid in securing impartial administration and lessen the number of people who, even in circumstances of dire need, will not apply for assistance because in their minds there is a stigma attached to it.
The legislation should make provision for the right of the applicant to appeal and, while it safeguards the interests of the person in need, should clarify the authority of the administration to give assistance.
The assistance given should be sufficient to maintain the health and welfare of the recipients. If society does not provide this minimum, the results of its policy will be physical, mental and social breakdown which will in the long rim be more costly to the community.
We in this group say amen to that statement of basic principles. Over the years the council has worked unobtrusively. It has had a devoted number of members, officers and governors interested in the problem and representing a cross section of Canada. The list of members for 1959-60 contains about a hundred names and I see the names of prominent industrialists, church people, people engaged in church work and social welfare work as well as well-known socialists, Liberals and Conservatives.
And well-known businessmen.

Yes. I give credit to these people who have a social conscience and who

recognize that this is a problem that must receive consideration, not only by governments but by organizations such as this and others throughout the country. Indeed, the problem has received consideration by farm organizations, women's organizations, labour organizations, other organizations and devoted individuals.
The Canadian welfare council published a policy statement adopted at the annual meeting held June 2, 1958. I understand the policy statement still stand's although more emphasis was contained in the final recommendation.
I referred to it this morning.
I am glad to know that for once I am following in the steps of the hon. member for Essex East instead of him following in mine.
We are walking along parallel roads.
I hope I am walking on the road to over-all social security.
I am walking on the road to Damascus.

The hon. member suggests that he has just seen the light. Not everyone will agree with these recommendations but I think it is worth while to read them. They are:
1.	The present universal flat rate pension commencing at age 70 should be retained.
2.	Consideration should be given to arrangements which would enable certain classes of people in the 65-69 age group to qualify for the old age security pension.
3.	Provision should be made for a continuing review and periodic consideration of adjustment in the amount of the universal flat rate pension on the basis of adequate statistical data relating to such important factors as minimum needs and levels of expenditure of older people.
4.	Financial assistance should be made available by the provinces to all persons 65 and over who are in need, with federal sharing of benefit costs.
5.	A joint parliamentary committee should be established to study the question of contributory wage-related old age benefits in addition to the universal pension and to make recommendations to parliament.
6.	Whether or not a compulsory contributory old age pension program is developed, the dominion government should lay down appropriate standards for private pension plans in connection with which income tax deductions are granted.
7.	There should be a federal public assistance act which would be, in effect, an extension of the Unemployment Assistance Act and which would enable the dominion government to share the aggregate costs to a province, and to the municipalities in a province, of providing financial assistance to all persons who are in need. The Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons' Allowances Act, and the Disabled Persons' Allowances Act should be incorporated as specific sections of this general public assistance act. The proposed act should, under these sections, provide the provinces with the option of continuing old age assistance,
Business of the House blind persons' allowances and disabled persons' allowances as separate programs, or of incorporating these categories in a generalized public assistance program with the same provisions respecting the sharing of costs as in the Unemployment Assistance Act.
8.	The operation of all public assistance programs should be based upon sound and clearly defined standards, particularly with respect to amount of assistance, etc.
9.	The basic assumptions underlying the Unemployment Insurance Act and the regulations pertaining to it should be reviewed in the light of experience and of changed conditions since the system was established and should, where necessary, be revised.
10.	Unemployment insurance coverage should be extended to include as many of the uncovered groups as possible.
11.	The ratio of benefits to earnings under the Unemployment Insurance Act should be increased. _ 12. The services provided by the unemployment insurance commission should be improved. Particular attention should be given to the need to strengthen the staff and administration, especially of the special placements section.
13.	More attention should be given to the problem of long term unemployed and marginal workers who find difficulty in obtaining satisfactory placements in a competitive labour market, but who may have the capacity and potential to profit from training.
14.	Adequate health services should be an Integral part of public assistance programs and as such, should be eligible for federal sharing of costs.
15.	Consideration should be given to the establishment of a cash sickness benefit program or programs.
16.	A program of benefits without a needs test should be instituted for dependent survivors.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
Progress reported.
